concepts/nudge.title: Nudge
concepts/nudge.content:
Nudge
Core idea
A Nudge is a behaviorally informed change to Choice Architecture that predictably steers behavior while preserving meaningful freedom to choose otherwise. The canonical boundary condition is that the chooser can still go another way: options remain available, economic incentives are not substantially changed, and avoidance is easy and cheap. This is the test supplied by Thaler and Sunstein in Nudge: The Final Edition.
The concept is most useful when it is kept narrow. A nudge is not every contextual feature that happens to influence behavior; it is a deliberate attempt to shape choice through the design of the choice environment. That intentionality matters because responsibility attaches to the architect once influence is deliberate, a point emphasized by Hansen and Jespersen in Nudge and the Manipulation of Choice.
Nudging should also not be mistaken for the whole of behavioral public policy. It is one important instrument in a wider toolkit, and it often works best when combined with taxes, subsidies, mandates, disclosure, enforcement, and regulation. Loewenstein and Chater make this policy-toolkit warning central in Putting Nudges in Perspective.
In digital environments, nudges appear in interface details such as defaults, reminders, prompts, ordering, salience, warnings, feedback, friction, recommendation structures, and simplified forms. But digital nudging can also exceed the classical model. When choice architecture becomes data-driven, personalized, dynamic, and continuously updated through feedback, it becomes a Hypernudge, as Yeung argues in Hypernudge: Big Data as a Mode of Regulation by Design.
The digital turn also opens a constructive possibility beyond nudging. Algorithms need not only steer users toward a predetermined target; they can sometimes help users deliberate, understand tradeoffs, and move toward their own considered judgments. This is the thought-partner direction developed by Ludwig and coauthors in Algorithms as a Vehicle to Reflective Equilibrium: Behavioral Economics 2.0.
For a synthesis of the concept and its ethical constraints, see Nudging and the Ethics of Nudging.
Key distinctions

Nudge vs mandate: a mandate requires or forbids action; a nudge preserves the option to go another way.
Nudge vs incentive: incentives change payoffs; nudges often work by changing attention, effort, salience, framing, or default status.
Nudge vs Sludge: a nudge should help users by their own lights; sludge uses friction to block or burden welfare-enhancing action.
Nudge vs boost: a boost improves competence or capability; a nudge changes the choice environment. Thaler and Sunstein argue that the two can and should often be combined.
Nudge vs policy mix: a nudge changes choice architecture, but a policy problem may also require incentives, regulation, legal duties, public provision, or enforcement.
Transparent nudge vs Manipulation: ethical nudging should be visible, publicly defensible, and compatible with reflective choice.
Type 1 vs type 2 nudge: nudge typology (Nudge) distinguishes nudges that influence automatic behavior from nudges that shape reflective choice.
Static nudge vs Hypernudge: static nudges arrange a relatively stable choice environment; hypernudges continuously reconfigure informational choice architecture using data and algorithms.
Nudge vs algorithmic thought partner: a nudge changes the environment of choice; a thought partner helps the user understand and reason about the choice.

Evidence and debate
The foundational evidence has three layers. First, nudges work because real choosers are not frictionless optimizers: they use heuristics, face self-control problems, respond to frames and defaults, and take cues from social environments. Nudge - Part I Humans and Econs supplies that behavioral mechanism layer.
Second, nudges are most useful under identifiable decision conditions: choices are difficult, rare, delayed in feedback, poorly mapped to outcomes, or easy to postpone. Nudge - Chapter 4 When Do We Need a Nudge is the course anchor for this diagnostic test.
Third, nudging becomes practical design through defaults, feedback, error tolerance, mappings, structured complexity, curated options, and salient incentives. Nudge - Introduction gives the foundational definition and examples; Nudge - Chapter 5 Choice Architecture gives the main design toolkit; and the EAST Framework gives a practitioner shorthand for many nudges and related behavioral interventions: Easy, Attractive, Social, and Timely.
The ethical debate begins with chooser welfare, autonomy, dignity, and self-government. Sunstein’s The Ethics of Influence: Government in the Age of Behavioral Science supplies that value vocabulary, including the “as judged by themselves” standard captured here as Chooser Welfare.
Schmidt and Engelen’s The Ethics of Nudging: An Overview is the review anchor for that debate. It shows why formal freedom of choice does not settle the matter: nudges may also affect volitional autonomy, rational agency, and freedom from domination.
The manipulation debate asks whether formal freedom to choose otherwise is enough. Nudges are used precisely where people are predictably fallible, so the practical question is whether users can notice, understand, and resist the nudge in context. Hansen and Jespersen develop this issue in Nudge and the Manipulation of Choice.
The policy debate asks whether nudging is sufficient. A behavioral cause can justify a traditional intervention, such as a tax or regulation; an economic problem can sometimes benefit from behavioral design; and many serious problems require hybrid packages. Loewenstein and Chater’s Putting Nudges in Perspective is the anchor for keeping nudges inside a wider behavioral-policy agenda.
The digital debate asks what happens when nudges are personalized, dynamic, and opaque. Classical tests such as opt-out, transparency, and consent become harder to apply when the choice environment is continuously modified. Yeung’s Hypernudge: Big Data as a Mode of Regulation by Design is the anchor for this problem.
The paradigm debate asks whether digital nudging should only make nudges more precise, or whether it should build tools that help users reach their own considered judgments. Behavioral Economics 2.0 (Algorithmic Thought Partners) names the latter direction.
The main debates concern welfare, autonomy, transparency, manipulation, and sufficiency. A nudge may be too weak for externalities or serious harms; a nudge may become manipulative if the user cannot understand or easily avoid it; and a nudge may serve the architect rather than the chooser.
Typology
The former nudge-typology page is now folded into this concept. A useful typology asks two questions. First, does the nudge work mainly through automatic cognition or reflective cognition? Second, can the person being nudged recognize the intervention and its purpose? This distinction matters because nudges that bypass awareness raise sharper concerns about manipulation, transparency, and autonomy.
Practical or policy relevance
In digital systems, nudges can improve welfare by helping users complete beneficial tasks, avoid errors, compare options, remember intentions, understand consequences, and resist harmful defaults. They can also be used for platform-serving goals such as retention, engagement, data capture, or upselling. The course should therefore ask not only “does it change behavior?” but “whose welfare does the design optimize, and how easy is it to resist?”
The policy-mix question is especially important online. If the problem is privacy exploitation, addictive design, manipulative subscription architecture, or data-driven discrimination, a digital nudge may need to be paired with consumer protection, privacy regulation, audit duties, competition policy, or limits on harmful defaults.

concepts/personalized-choice-architectur.title: Personalized Choice Architecture
concepts/personalized-choice-architectur.content:
Personalized Choice Architecture
Core idea
Personalized Choice Architecture is a digital choice environment tailored to a particular user or group through data, profiles, predictions, and inferred preferences. Personalization is one of the decisive features that separates digital nudging from static nudges: the same interface need not present the same options, defaults, timing, friction, or explanations to every chooser. Yeung’s Hypernudge: Big Data as a Mode of Regulation by Design is the anchor for that digital shift.
Personalization can make interventions more relevant and less burdensome. It can also make influence harder to detect, compare, resist, or govern.
The central welfare distinction is between predicting susceptibility and supporting judgment. Personalizing which nudge works best is not the same as personalizing the decision target to the user’s considered judgment. Ludwig and coauthors’ Algorithms as a Vehicle to Reflective Equilibrium: Behavioral Economics 2.0 is the anchor for this difference.
Personalized nudging is now treated as a special case of personalized choice architecture. Mills’s Personalized Nudging (Mills) makes the taxonomy more systematic: the nudge can personalize the delivery mechanism, the content or target, or both.
Mechanisms

User profiling: the system infers interests, habits, risks, vulnerabilities, or likely responses.
Contextual targeting: prompts and rankings change with location, time, device, prior behavior, or surrounding conditions.
Personalized salience: some options are made more visible or credible for one user than another.
Personalized defaults: the system chooses what happens if a specific user does nothing.
Personalized friction: the system can make refusal, exit, or comparison easier for some users and harder for others.
Personalized thought partnership: the system helps the user clarify options, preferences, constraints, and psychological traps.

Delivery vs content personalization
The most important operational distinction is between two forms of personalization:

Delivery personalization: personalizing how the nudge is delivered, such as mechanism, timing, format, channel, or frame.
Content or target personalization: personalizing what the person is nudged toward, such as the selected default, option, date, product, behavior, or contribution rate.

This distinction is central for digital nudging because the two forms have different welfare and accountability implications. Delivery personalization can be a tactic for effectiveness. Target personalization is a claim about what is good for this user.
Precision nudging
Precision nudging is also folded into this page. It names the use of data, machine learning, or AI to select which nudge, timing, format, or target is most likely to produce a desired behavioral outcome for a given person or group. Its promise is fit; its danger is that the system may personalize for compliance, conversion, or engagement rather than chooser welfare.
Ethical significance
Personalized choice architecture complicates Chooser Welfare. A platform may claim to give users what they want, but the evidence for that claim may come from behavior that the platform itself shaped. It also complicates fairness: users may face different choice sets, prices, warnings, opportunities, or barriers without knowing that others see something else.
The privacy issue is structural. Personalization depends on data collection, inference, and repurposing. Strong personalization therefore links digital nudging to Privacy and Consent and Algorithmic Fairness.
The welfare issue is equally structural. A system can personalize for persuasion, convenience, engagement, or reflective equilibrium (Algorithmic Thought Partners). These are not the same target.
Digital relevance
Examples include social feeds, product recommendations, search results, navigation suggestions, health prompts, ad targeting, personalized prices, app onboarding, notification timing, and privacy defaults.
Personalization is not automatically manipulative. It becomes troubling when the user cannot understand the basis of the intervention, when the target is vulnerability rather than welfare, or when the system optimizes for the architect’s interests under the language of relevance or convenience.

concepts/prediction-policy-problems.title: Prediction Policy Problems
concepts/prediction-policy-problems.content:
Prediction Policy Problems
Core idea
Prediction Policy Problems are decisions that hinge on predicting an outcome rather than estimating the causal effect of an intervention. The policy question is not primarily “what does this treatment do?” but “which person, case, option, or situation is most likely to have the relevant outcome?”
In the course sequence, this concept generalizes the bail example. A judge deciding whom to release, a doctor deciding whom to test, a platform deciding what to recommend, a tax authority deciding which returns to audit, and a job seeker deciding which openings to apply to can all involve prediction policy problems.
Key distinctions

Prediction versus causation: if the decision changes the payoff conditional on a predicted outcome, prediction is central; if the decision changes the outcome itself, causal inference is central.
Ranking versus treatment effect: many prediction policy problems are ranking problems in which welfare improves when high-risk, high-benefit, or high-need cases are prioritized correctly.
Prediction accuracy versus policy value: accurate prediction matters only through the decision and payoff function it supports.
Algorithmic aid versus automation: prediction policy problems often call for decision support rather than replacement of human judgment.
Evaluation versus construction: building the predictor can be comparatively easy; evaluating whether it improves decisions can be difficult.

Evidence and debate
Prediction policy problems matter because many high-stakes decisions are already rankings under uncertainty. The question is who should be prioritized, released, tested, audited, helped, warned, or shown an option first. Mullainathan’s Economics in the Age of Algorithms makes this one of the central reasons algorithms should matter to economics.
The canonical empirical example is bail. Human Decisions and Machine Predictions asks whether machine predictions can improve judicial release decisions by identifying risk more accurately than human decision-makers. The point of the example is not that automation is intrinsically superior, but that misranking can be costly when human decisions are noisy and inconsistent.
The public-policy promise is that better ranking can create large welfare gains without expanding the underlying policy. The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Algorithms gives that effectiveness frame: algorithmic interventions can have high apparent returns when they are aimed at decisions that are badly misranked.
The implementation problem is fragility. A prediction policy problem can look solved if one ignores missing counterfactual outcomes, omitted values, local workflow, human overrides, or strategic responses. Fragile Algorithms and Fallible Decision-Makers explains why algorithmic decision support can fail even when the predictive model looks strong.
The concept is inseparable from selective labels (Algorithmic Policy Efficiency) and omitted payoff bias (Algorithmic Policy Efficiency). These are economic and econometric problems, not merely computational ones: the available labels may depend on earlier human decisions, and the measured payoff may omit outcomes the policy actually cares about.
Practical or policy relevance
For Digital Nudging, prediction policy problems describe many algorithmic choice architectures: recommender systems, triage tools, fraud alerts, safety prompts, benefit targeting, consumer decision aids, and AI assistants. These systems decide what to show, when to intervene, whom to prioritize, and what explanation to provide.
The digital-nudging question is therefore not just whether a prediction is accurate. It is whether the prediction-guided workflow improves welfare, preserves agency, handles omitted values, and remains contestable.
Related pages

concepts/privacy-and-consent.title: Privacy and Consent
concepts/privacy-and-consent.content:
Privacy and Consent
Core idea
Privacy and Consent concerns the collection, processing, repurposing, and behavioral use of personal data in digital choice architecture. Privacy is not only about secrecy or data control; it is also about how personal data enables continuous, personalized influence. Yeung’s Hypernudge: Big Data as a Mode of Regulation by Design is the anchor for that wider behavioral view of privacy.
Notice and consent problem
Notice-and-consent models are weak when data ecosystems are dynamic, cumulative, and hard to understand. Users rarely read or understand privacy policies, privacy harms accumulate across services and time, and Big Data value often comes from unexpected future uses that could not be specified clearly at collection. Yeung develops this critique for Big Data hypernudging.
The problem is not solved by clicking “I agree.” Consent to broad data processing does not automatically authorize deception, manipulation, or behavioral experimentation.
The dark-pattern literature makes the same point at the interface level. Consent can be formally collected through screens that hide refusal, overload the user, preselect extractive options, use confusing wording, or make privacy-protective choices harder to complete. In that setting, the legal event of consent may be present while meaningful consent is absent.
Dark patterns in consent design
Consent design can extract data by making privacy-protective action harder than privacy-invasive action. Dark Patterns at Scale identifies forced enrollment and privacy-invasive design as part of the e-commerce dark-pattern landscape. Dark Patterns: Past, Present, and Future connects these interface tactics to the broader history of privacy-invasive growth hacking and behavioral exploitation. An Ontology of Dark Patterns Knowledge places Privacy Zuckering, privacy mazes, forced communication or disclosure, and related consent patterns within a broader ontology of forced action, obstruction, and interface interference.
Privacy loss is a distinct harm, not merely a side effect of monetary loss or bad information. A design can be troubling even if the immediate monetary cost is small, because it extracts data, weakens consent, and expands future opportunities for personalization, targeting, and behavioral experimentation. What Makes a Dark Pattern… Dark? is the anchor for separating privacy loss from other dark-pattern harms.
The regulatory question is whether consent remains valid when the interface has been optimized to make refusal hard, confusing, or socially pressured. Dark pattern regulation (Dark Patterns) connects these design issues to data-protection regimes such as GDPR.
Empirical work also matters because consent interfaces can be mildly manipulative rather than blatantly deceptive. Shining a Light on Dark Patterns shows why subtle design changes can affect acceptance while avoiding the backlash that makes users recognize the pressure.
Digital relevance
Digital nudges often depend on data. Recommendation systems, targeted prompts, personalized defaults, adaptive friction, behavioral ads, and A/B tests all require information about users or populations.
That makes privacy a design constraint, not merely a compliance notice. The course should ask what data is collected, what inferences are drawn, how data is repurposed, whether users can understand or refuse the use, and whether the resulting choice architecture serves user welfare.
Personalized public-interest nudging can also create a data-access problem. Some personalized nudges can use simple data, but richer personalization may require data held by private firms, raising questions about data trusts, data commons, stewardship, privacy, security, and trust. Mills’s Personalized Nudging (Mills) is the anchor for that public-policy version of the problem.
Data is not only a precondition for digital nudging; it can be the thing extracted by the nudge. Consent banners, account registration, personalization prompts, and permission requests should therefore be evaluated as choice architectures in their own right.

concepts/recommendation-systems.title: Recommendation Systems
concepts/recommendation-systems.content:
Recommendation Systems
Core idea
Recommendation Systems are algorithmic systems that select, rank, filter, or suggest options for users. In Digital Nudging, they are a major form of informational Choice Architecture because they shape which options become visible, salient, credible, easy, or seemingly relevant.
The core mechanism is guidance without formal coercion. Search engines, product recommendation engines, navigation systems, and feeds do not force users to choose, but they channel attention and choice through ranking and suggestion. Yeung’s Hypernudge: Big Data as a Mode of Regulation by Design treats these systems as Big Data decision-guidance.
The main conceptual distinction is between predicting likely behavior and supporting better judgment. Traditional recommenders predict what a user or similar users would choose; algorithmic thought partners should help the user decide what they would choose under better information and reflection. Ludwig and coauthors develop that contrast in Algorithms as a Vehicle to Reflective Equilibrium: Behavioral Economics 2.0.
The welfare warning is that behavior can be a bad proxy for what users actually want. Recommendation systems that optimize engagement may infer the wrong target from behavior, a problem developed by Kleinberg and coauthors in The Challenge of Understanding What Users Want.
Mechanisms

Ranking: ordering options so some are more likely to be noticed or chosen.
Filtering: hiding or demoting options before the user sees them.
Prediction: inferring what a user is likely to want, click, buy, watch, or share.
Salience: making selected items stand out as relevant, popular, urgent, nearby, or recommended.
Feedback: using the user’s response to update future recommendations.

Ethical significance
Recommendation systems often present themselves as helpful personalization, but their objectives may be mixed. A recommender may optimize for relevance, revenue, engagement, sponsored placement, retention, safety, public value, or institutional convenience. Users often cannot tell which objective is operative.
This makes recommendation systems central to Transparency and Disclosure, Privacy and Consent, Algorithmic Fairness, Manipulation, and Chooser Welfare.
The Behavioral Economics 2.0 challenge is that predicting observed choice can amplify mistakes. A recommender that accurately predicts impulsive, biased, or confused behavior may be technically successful while welfare-defeating.
This is the heart of the Behavior-Welfare Gap for recommendation systems. Prediction quality, engagement, and user welfare can come apart. The more a recommender is framed as a choice aid, the more it needs explanation, welfare-sensitive objectives, and evidence beyond observed behavior.
Digital relevance
Examples include search results, social feeds, video recommendations, product recommendations, app-store rankings, navigation suggestions, news feeds, dating matches, job ads, credit offers, and public-service triage tools.
The course should treat recommendation systems as active choice architecture, not neutral information delivery.
Related pages

Hypernudge

Personalized Choice Architecture

Transparency and Disclosure

Open questions

concepts/shrouded-attributes.title: Shrouded Attributes
concepts/shrouded-attributes.content:
Shrouded Attributes
Core idea
Shrouded Attributes are product or service features that are important for welfare but hidden, delayed, de-emphasized, or made difficult to evaluate at the moment of choice. Typical examples include add-on prices, fees, penalties, renewal terms, usage costs, privacy costs, and cancellation burdens.
The basic market failure is that shrouding can persist even under competition. If some consumers are myopic or unaware, firms can advertise a cheap base good while profiting from expensive add-ons. Shrouded Attributes, Consumer Myopia, and Information Suppression in Competitive Markets is the anchor for that mechanism.
Key distinctions

Hidden information vs shrouded information: shrouding need not make information impossible to find; it makes it practically absent from the choice moment.
Base good vs add-on: the advertised product may be cheap while later complementary costs are high.
Myopic consumers vs sophisticated consumers: myopes ignore add-ons; sophisticates anticipate and avoid them.
Shrouding vs sludge: shrouding hides or de-emphasizes attributes; sludge makes action costly. Many digital designs use both.
Competition vs debiasing: competition may not reveal shrouded terms because educating consumers can fail to benefit the educating firm.

Evidence and debate
The “curse of debiasing” explains why firms may not compete by educating consumers. A consumer educated about hidden add-ons can take advantage of another firm’s low base price while avoiding add-ons, so the educating firm may not win the customer. Gabaix and Laibson supply this explanation.
The disclosure problem is that making information technically available does not guarantee that users can use it. Disclosure can fail when attention, motivation, complexity, or overload prevent effective uptake, as Disclosure: Psychology Changes Everything emphasizes.
The choice-aid response is to make hidden attributes usable at the moment of decision. AI choice engines can surface total costs, translate terms, compare add-ons, and warn about hidden burdens. Sunstein’s Behavioral Biases, Choice Engines, and Paternalistic AI treats shrouded attributes as a central reason to build and regulate such tools.
Practical or policy relevance
Digital environments make shrouding easier to implement and test. A website can highlight a base price, hide fees until late in checkout, bury renewal terms, obscure privacy costs, or make cancellation consequences hard to see.
For AI as Choice Aid, shrouded attributes are the canonical case for defensive assistance. A user-serving tool can surface total costs, translate terms, compare add-ons, and warn about hidden burdens. This is closely related to adaptive armor (Algorithmic Thought Partners).
Related pages

AI as Choice Aid
Smart Disclosure
Dark Patterns
Sludge
Behavior-Welfare Gap

Open questions
When should law require unshrouding directly, and when should it require data access so user-side tools can unshroud on the user’s behalf?

concepts/sludge.title: Sludge
concepts/sludge.content:
Sludge
Core idea
Sludge is friction in Choice Architecture that makes it harder for people to obtain outcomes that would make them better off by their own lights. It is the negative counterpart of the “make it easy” principle in Nudge: The Final Edition.
In digital settings, sludge often appears as confusing forms, hidden opt-outs, difficult cancellation paths, burdensome consent controls, unnecessary identity checks, long disclosures, shrouded fees, or asymmetric flows that make entry easy and exit hard.
In the dark-pattern cluster, sludge should be treated as a method, not the whole definition. Dark Patterns may use sludge, but they can also work through urgency, scarcity, social proof, trick questions, hidden costs, bad defaults, or emotional pressure. The deeper problem is not friction alone; it is friction used as adversarial choice architecture (Dark Patterns).
Key distinctions

Sludge vs nudge: a nudge should help users choose well; sludge burdens beneficial action or easy exit.
Intentional vs incidental sludge: firms may design retention friction on purpose, while agencies may produce burden through program-integrity rules or legacy processes.
Protective friction vs exploitative friction: some friction prevents fraud, error, or impulsive harm; exploitative friction serves the architect at the user’s expense.
Administrative burden vs dark pattern: administrative burden can occur in public or private bureaucracy; dark patterns are manipulative interface designs, many of which work through sludge.
Sludge reduction vs deregulation: reducing unnecessary burden does not mean eliminating all eligibility, security, or deliberation safeguards.
Sludge as method vs dark pattern as strategy: sludge names friction; dark patterns name the extractive or autonomy-undermining use of interface architecture.

Evidence and debate
Sludge analysis begins by treating time, confusion, paperwork, abandonment, and exclusion as real costs. Subscription cancellation, mail-in rebates, shrouded attributes, travel reimbursement rules, college admissions, TSA PreCheck, cookie consent, and tax filing are all examples where formal availability can coexist with practical burden. Nudge - Chapter 8 Sludge develops the concept through these cases and links sludge reduction to Smart Disclosure, because better data and simpler forms can reduce burden.
The central debate is when friction is justified. Digital governance needs a cost-benefit account that includes users’ time, confusion, abandonment, and exclusion. The EAST Framework supplies the practical inverse: good interventions often begin by finding and reducing cognitive or practical friction.
Sludge is not only inefficient friction. It can undermine autonomy, dignity, and chooser welfare when it exhausts, confuses, or traps people. Sunstein’s The Ethics of Influence: Government in the Age of Behavioral Science supplies the value vocabulary for that normative diagnosis. In some cases, sludge becomes a mechanism of Manipulation.
The dark-pattern literature makes sludge concrete at the interface level. Obstruction includes roach motel designs, added steps, privacy mazes, price comparison prevention, and hard-to-cancel flows. Gray et al. identify obstruction as a high-level strategy; Mathur et al. document hard-to-cancel flows in e-commerce; Gray et al. place these cases within a broader ontology; and Luguri and Strahilevitz show that obstruction can materially increase acceptance or signup behavior.
The broader dark-pattern frame explains why sludge is often tied to extraction rather than mere bad usability. Dark Patterns: Past, Present, and Future connects obstruction to growth hacking and behavioral exploitation, while What Makes a Dark Pattern… Dark? helps separate the harms of sludge into welfare loss, autonomy loss, privacy loss, and regulatory evasion.
Practical or policy relevance
Sludge is central to digital nudging because many digital harms are not explicit prohibitions but practical barriers. A privacy setting may exist but be buried; a subscription may be cancellable but only through a long flow; a benefit may be available but hidden behind a confusing website. Sludge analysis asks whether formal choice is meaningful in practice.
The ethics framework adds a proprietary-systems warning: the firm that controls the interface may also control the data needed to measure abandonment, confusion, and asymmetry between acceptance and refusal.
Adaptive systems make the warning sharper. Sludge can be tested, personalized, and optimized, turning friction into a learned instrument of steering. Yeung’s Hypernudge: Big Data as a Mode of Regulation by Design is the anchor for that data-driven extension.
For the dark-pattern module, sludge is the clearest way to show how an interface can preserve a formal right while defeating its practical exercise. A user may be free to cancel, refuse tracking, compare prices, or decline an upsell, but only after navigating costs deliberately imposed by the architect.

concepts/smart-disclosure.title: Smart Disclosure
concepts/smart-disclosure.content:
Smart Disclosure
Core idea
Smart Disclosure is a strategy for turning formally available information into usable comparison infrastructure. The problem is not simply that users lack information. It is that complex choices often require standardized product data, access to one’s own usage history, and software-mediated comparison before disclosure can actually improve decisions.
The basic move is to release complex information in standardized, machine-readable form so that choice engines, apps, intermediaries, or AI tools can search, filter, compare, and recommend. In Nudge: The Final Edition, this makes disclosure part of Choice Architecture: the goal is not more text, but better mappings between options and welfare.
Figure SD.1 separates ordinary disclosure from smart disclosure. The first makes information formally available and then leaves the user to find, parse, compare, and act on it. The second treats disclosure as infrastructure for comparison: standardized product data, personal usage data, and choice engines work together to reduce comparison friction.

  
  Figure SD.1. Smart disclosure as choice infrastructure. Smart disclosure is not more text; it is the conversion of product and usage data into machine-readable comparison, sense-making, and usable guidance.

Key distinctions

Formal disclosure vs usable disclosure: information can be disclosed yet remain practically unreadable.
Human-readable vs machine-readable: machine-readable disclosure allows decision tools to compare complex products and services.
Product data vs usage data: smart disclosure requires both standardized product attributes and user access to their own histories.
Choice engines vs static labels: choice engines use data to search, filter, compare, and recommend.
Transparency vs steering: smart disclosure can empower users, but the tools built on it need governance because rankings and recommendations can be self-serving.

Evidence and debate
Smart disclosure starts from the failure of ordinary disclosure. Information can be technically available while remaining practically useless because users miss it, distrust it, lack motivation to process it, or cannot compare it across options. Loewenstein and coauthors make this psychological case in Disclosure: Psychology Changes Everything.
The empirical mechanism is comparison friction (Smart Disclosure): the wedge between available comparative information and actual comparison behavior. Kling and coauthors show this in the Medicare Part D setting, where personalized cost information changed plan switching and reduced costs even though the relevant information was already formally available in Comparison Friction.
The smart-disclosure response is data infrastructure: product attributes and personal usage data must be standardized, portable, timely, and machine-readable enough for tools to make comparison feasible. Nudge - Chapter 7 Smart Disclosure develops this through phone plans, fuel economy, APR standardization, online terms, travel websites, Open Banking, energy-choice apps, grocery allergens, and platform usage histories.
The main debate is whether this infrastructure empowers users or merely relocates influence to new intermediaries. Choice engines and recommendation systems can be user-serving, but they can also become hypernudges if ranking, salience, and selection are optimized for the architect’s interests. Yeung’s Hypernudge: Big Data as a Mode of Regulation by Design gives the warning.
The AI version goes beyond comparison toward sense-making. Algorithmic tools can translate complex terms, surface shrouded attributes, flag hidden costs, and help users reason through consequences. This makes smart disclosure part of adaptive armor (Algorithmic Thought Partners), not only data release; Ludwig and coauthors develop that constructive direction in Algorithms as a Vehicle to Reflective Equilibrium: Behavioral Economics 2.0.
Practical or policy relevance
Smart disclosure is highly relevant to digital nudging because many digital choices are too complex for static labels. Machine-readable data can support comparison tools for banking, energy, subscriptions, insurance, health plans, app privacy, algorithmic recommendations, and platform terms.
The governance question is whether the data infrastructure empowers the user or simply supplies better inputs for personalized steering. Smart disclosure needs rules for data quality, standardization, portability, security, tool incentives, ranking logic, explanation, and contestability.
For AI as Choice Aid, smart disclosure is infrastructure rather than a complete solution. The user-facing layer still has to make the data understandable, balanced, trustworthy, and action-guiding.

concepts/transparency-and-disclosure.title: Transparency and Disclosure
concepts/transparency-and-disclosure.content:
Transparency and Disclosure
Core idea
Transparency and Disclosure collects the course’s vocabulary for making choice architecture visible, intelligible, contestable, and publicly accountable. Transparency asks whether affected people and publics can understand the action, reason, and relevant effects of an intervention. Disclosure is one instrument for transparency, but disclosure can fail when information is too long, complex, badly timed, or strategically buried.
This page absorbs the former page on transparency and publicity and the former page on reasoned transparency. The distinction matters: ethical digital nudging needs both user-facing clarity and institutional reason-giving.
Publicity, epistemic transparency, and disclosure
Publicity is an ethical test, not merely a notice requirement. A nudge should be visible enough, publicly defensible, and compatible with autonomy, dignity, welfare, and self-government. Sunstein’s The Ethics of Influence: Government in the Age of Behavioral Science supplies this publicity standard.
Epistemic transparency is narrower and more immediate: can the target recognize the intervention and its purpose while choosing? A nudge may be publicly announced while the target still cannot recognize its intention or mechanism in context. Hansen and Jespersen’s Nudge and the Manipulation of Choice is the anchor for this distinction between public defensibility and transparency at the point of influence.
Transparency also matters because it controls power. In Schmidt and Engelen’s overview, the non-domination worry is that nudging can give architects uncontrolled influence over citizens or users. The response is not mere notice, but transparency plus democratic control, accountability, and contestability.
Disclosure is weaker still. A cookie notice, terms page, or long explanation may disclose information without making it practically usable. The course should therefore ask whether disclosure becomes understanding, and whether understanding arrives at the right time.
Fishbowl and reasoned transparency
Algorithmic governance needs a second distinction: access to institutional materials is not the same as an explanation of reasons. Fishbowl transparency is access to records, code, data, logs, documents, meetings, and other evidence of what an institution did. Reasoned transparency is the why: the objective, justification, design choice, validation, limits, and role of a system in the decision. Coglianese and Lehr develop this distinction in Transparency and Algorithmic Governance.
Digital nudging needs both. Users may need a simple reason why a recommendation, default, warning, price, ranking, or friction appeared. Regulators may need fishbowl access to experiments, objectives, data flows, and audit trails. The public may need a reasoned explanation of why the system’s behavioral influence is legitimate.
The digital-nudging application is the vault’s course interpretation of Coglianese and Lehr’s administrative-law distinction.
Digital relevance
Digital nudging makes transparency difficult because the relevant choice architecture may be dynamic, personalized, experimental, proprietary, or algorithmic. A user may see the interface while not knowing which options were hidden, which ranking rule applied, why a default was selected, or what objective was optimized.
For hypernudges, transparency must also be temporal. A system that changes continuously needs records of what changed, who was exposed, what metric was optimized, and what effects were observed.
Yeung’s Hypernudge: Big Data as a Mode of Regulation by Design is the anchor for that problem: data-driven choice architecture can be personalized and continuously modified while remaining difficult for users and outsiders to reconstruct.

Open questions

Who or what it is
Arunesh Mathur is a computer scientist and privacy/HCI researcher whose work in this vault focuses on dark patterns, online manipulation, and the measurement of exploitative interface design.
Why it matters here
Mathur’s work supplies both the empirical and normative spine of the dark-pattern cluster. Dark Patterns at Scale documents dark patterns across shopping websites, while What Makes a Dark Pattern… Dark? asks how to connect design attributes to welfare, autonomy, collective harms, and regulatory objectives.

entities/arvind-narayanan.content:
Arvind Narayanan
Who or what it is
Arvind Narayanan is a computer scientist and scholar of algorithmic accountability, privacy, machine learning ethics, and dark patterns. In this vault, he enters through What If Algorithmic Fairness Is a Category Error?, Dark Patterns at Scale, and Dark Patterns: Past, Present, and Future.
Why it matters here
Narayanan supplies the strongest current corrective to metric-centered algorithmic fairness in the course sequence. His contribution is to reframe fairness as a property of sociotechnical decision systems and algorithmic bureaucracies rather than of predictive models alone.
In the dark-pattern module, Narayanan’s coauthored work helps frame dark patterns as a convergence of behavioral nudging, retail deception, growth hacking, and A/B-tested extraction.

The Behavioural Insights Team is an applied behavioral science organization associated with the development and diffusion of behavioral insights in policy and practice. Why it matters here

Cass R. Sunstein
Who or what it is
Cass R. Sunstein is a legal scholar, behavioral public policy theorist, and coauthor, with Richard H. Thaler, of Nudge: The Final Edition. In the book’s front matter, he is described as a Harvard Law School professor and former administrator of the White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs.
Why it matters here
Sunstein connects nudging to law, regulation, disclosure, administrative burden, algorithmic governance, and the ethics of public choice architecture. The Ethics of Influence: Government in the Age of Behavioral Science is especially relevant to digital nudging because it frames influence through welfare, autonomy, dignity, self-government, Transparency and Disclosure, and Manipulation. Governing by Algorithm? extends the administrative-law side by asking when algorithms can reduce noise and cognitive bias in public decision-making.

index.content:
Digital Nudging Wiki
Digital nudging begins from a simple premise: digital environments are choice architectures. Defaults, friction, rankings, recommendations, warnings, consent flows, experiments, and AI assistants do not merely present options; they organize attention, effort, expectations, and opportunity. The wiki foregrounds five synthesis threads. Nudging and ethics defines the basic normative vocabulary. AI as choice aid asks when digital systems can help users reason through complex or adversarial choices. Dark patterns tracks the extraction-oriented mirror image of nudging. Predictive algorithms, bias, and fairness examines scoring, ranking, and decision support. Algorithmic governance asks how these systems can remain lawful, accountable, and humanly answerable.

How to use this wiki
This is a course-building wiki, not a finished textbook. The synthesis pages give the argument at lecture scale; concept pages define reusable vocabulary; source notes preserve what each paper or book contributes; unit notes turn larger sources into teachable chunks. The concept layer has been deliberately compressed: many useful subterms now live as sections or aliases inside the larger concepts rather than as separate pages.

sources/angwin-et-al.,-2016.title: Angwin et al., 2016
sources/angwin-et-al.,-2016.content:
Angwin et al., 2016: Machine Bias
Summary
Machine Bias is the ProPublica investigation that made the COMPAS controversy (Algorithmic Fairness) a canonical entry point for Algorithmic Fairness. It studies risk scores assigned to more than 7,000 people arrested in Broward County, Florida, and argues that the scores were racially skewed in their mistakes even when overall error rates looked similar.
The article is useful for the course because it makes algorithmic fairness concrete before the mathematics begins. A score that looks like neutral decision support can become a nudge or pressure on judges, probation officers, and pretrial decision-makers. It shapes attention, frames risk, and can move coercive public decisions while remaining partly hidden behind proprietary software.
Key claims

Risk assessment tools were spreading across pretrial release, sentencing, parole, and correctional supervision, often before strong independent validation.
In the Broward County data, COMPAS had limited predictive performance. Violent recidivism predictions were especially weak, while broader recidivism predictions were only modestly useful.
The racial disparity appeared in the type of error: Black defendants were more likely to be falsely labeled high risk, while white defendants were more likely to be falsely labeled low risk.
The disparity did not disappear when the analysis controlled for age, gender, prior criminal history, current charge, and observed recidivism.
The tool did not explicitly ask for race, but many inputs and background variables can still reflect racialized social structure.
Proprietary scoring created due-process and accountability problems because defendants and the public could not inspect the full calculation.

Evidence and methods
ProPublica obtained COMPAS scores for Broward County defendants arrested in 2013 and 2014, then checked subsequent criminal charges over a two-year period. The article pairs statistical analysis with narrative cases, especially Brisha Borden and Vernon Prater, to show how the same score can appear objective while producing sharply different error burdens across groups.
The investigation also reports institutional context: risk assessments were used in multiple legal settings, the software vendor disputed ProPublica’s analysis, and judges sometimes treated risk scores as relevant even when the tool’s creator warned against using them as the sole basis for sentencing.
Why it matters for Digital Nudging
This article starts the algorithmic fairness module with a governance problem that is close to digital nudging: algorithmic systems can influence human decisions without formally deciding anything themselves. COMPAS is not a recommender system in the platform sense, but it steers decision-makers through risk labels, salience, and institutional trust in scores.
For digital nudging, the key lesson is that algorithmic choice architecture must be evaluated by how its errors are distributed, who can contest it, which decision points it enters, and whether proprietary opacity prevents public justification. This directly connects to Hypernudge, Algorithmic Fairness, Transparency and Disclosure, and later work on dark patterns, recommender systems, and automated personalization.
Links into the wiki

COMPAS controversy (Algorithmic Fairness): the central case produced by this investigation.
fairness metrics (Algorithmic Fairness): explains why ProPublica’s focus on asymmetric error rates differs from calibration-based defenses.
risk assessment in criminal justice (Algorithmic Fairness): situates COMPAS in bail, sentencing, parole, and treatment decisions.
Algorithmic Fairness: the course sub-hub for the fairness branch.

Open questions

Which later responses best reconstruct the debate between ProPublica and Northpointe?
How should the course connect COMPAS to non-carceral platform systems such as ranking, feeds, credit scoring, and personalization?
How much statistical detail should be taught before introducing the normative question of which errors matter most?

Bibliographic reference
Angwin, J., Larson, J., Kirchner, L., & Mattu, S. (2016, May 23). Machine bias. ProPublica. www.propublica.org/article/machine-bias-risk-assessments-in-criminal-sentencing

sources/behavioural-insights-team,-2024.title: Behavioural Insights Team, 2024
sources/behavioural-insights-team,-2024.content:
Behavioural Insights Team, 2024: EAST: Four Simple Ways to Apply Behavioural Insights
Summary
EAST: Four Simple Ways to Apply Behavioural Insights is a revised and updated Behavioural Insights Team handbook for designing practical behavioral interventions. It condenses intervention design into four characteristics: make the target behavior Easy, Attractive, Social, and Timely. The report is deliberately pragmatic: it is meant to help practitioners generate and refine ideas, not to replace diagnosis, fieldwork, co-design, or evaluation.
For this vault, the source is best used as a quick reference for the properties of effective behavioral interventions. It complements Nudge: The Final Edition by translating nudging and Choice Architecture into an applied checklist.
Key claims

Effective interventions should reduce cognitive and practical effort. Defaults, fewer steps, simpler messages, and redesigned forms can have large effects because small friction costs often suppress action.
Effective interventions should attract attention and frame behavior carefully. Salience, personalization, timely prompts, environmental cues, and well-designed incentives can change what people notice and how they interpret a choice.
Effective interventions should use social forces with care. Descriptive norms, injunctive norms, networks, reciprocity, and operational transparency can help, but social information can backfire when the reference group is wrong or the norm reveals that undesirable behavior is common.
Effective interventions should meet people at the right moment. Timing matters across the day, week, life course, and moments of disruption. Good interventions consider immediate costs and benefits and help people form concrete plans.
EAST is not a complete methodology. The report explicitly says applied behavioral science also requires understanding context, testing assumptions, and using robust evaluation where possible.
The 2024 revision is more cautious than a simple greatest-hits list: it flags replication problems, failed effects, and behavioral pitfalls.

Evidence and methods
The handbook synthesizes behavioral science evidence, field experiments, and applied case studies. It emphasizes randomized controlled trials when feasible, but also notes that RCTs are not the only evaluation option.
The report’s recurring methodological advice is to study the behavioral context before designing the intervention. BIT recommends fieldwork, attention to user experience, co-design with people who deliver and use services, and evaluation of whether an intervention works in the actual setting.
Selected examples useful for teaching:

Easy: workplace pension auto-enrollment, green energy defaults, quick enrollment, simpler court summons forms, and university application assistance.
Attractive: salient prompts, framing, built-environment cues, commitment savings products, deposit contracts, prosocial incentives, and gamification.
Social: norm messages, peer comparison, network seeding, reciprocity in organ donation messages, and operational transparency.
Timely: Ramadan diabetes screening, fresh-start timing, Save More Tomorrow, implementation intentions, and jobseeker action planning.

Why it matters for Digital Nudging
EAST is immediately usable for digital nudging because most digital interventions can be checked against its four dimensions. Interfaces can make action easy through defaults, one-click flows, autofill, plain language, and reduced Sludge. They can make action attractive through salience, personalization, framing, and feedback. They can make action social through norm information, reputation cues, sharing, visible participation, and network effects. They can make action timely through notifications, reminders, fresh-start moments, just-in-time prompts, and planning tools.
The report is also a useful guardrail. It cautions that behavioral ideas do not travel automatically across contexts, that social norms and incentives can backfire, and that some once-promising effects fail to replicate. For digital nudging, that means EAST should be treated as a design checklist plus an evaluation prompt, not as a recipe book.
Links into the wiki

EAST Framework: compact quick reference distilled from the report.
Choice Architecture: EAST operationalizes choice architecture as an intervention-design checklist.
Nudge: EAST gives practical characteristics of effective nudges and related behavioral interventions.
Defaults: defaults are a central “Easy” tool.
Sludge: friction reduction is the inverse of sludge.
Digital Nudging: digital interfaces are natural settings for EAST-style intervention design.

Open questions

How should EAST be adapted for personalized, AI-mediated, or recommender-driven interventions?
When does making a behavior easy become insufficiently deliberative, especially for privacy, consent, or high-stakes decisions?
Which EAST interventions remain effective when users recognize them as nudges or encounter them repeatedly?

Bibliographic reference
Behavioural Insights Team. (2024). EAST: Four simple ways to apply behavioural insights (Revised and updated ed.). Behavioural Insights Ltd. www.bi.team/publications/east-four-simple-ways-to-apply-behavioural-insights/

sources/bhargava-et-al.,-2017.title: Bhargava et al., 2017
sources/bhargava-et-al.,-2017.content:
Bhargava et al., 2017: Choose to Lose: Health Plan Choices from a Menu with Dominated Options
Summary
Choose to Lose studies health insurance choices in a setting where many options were financially dominated by otherwise equivalent high-deductible plans. Because the plans differed only in cost-sharing and premium, the case provides an unusually clean test of whether people make financially sensible insurance choices.
The main finding is stark: most employees chose dominated plans. These choices produced meaningful excess spending, were more common among low-income employees, and usually did not self-correct through later switching. The authors argue that the pattern is best explained by low insurance competence rather than by ordinary risk preferences, informed preference for low deductibles, or mere menu complexity.
Key claims

Revealed insurance choices can reflect misunderstanding rather than risk preferences.
In the studied firm, 61% of employees chose nominally dominated plans and about 55% chose dominated plans after tax adjustment.
Employees in dominated plans could have saved an average of about $372 per year by moving to the otherwise equivalent high-deductible alternative.
Low-income employees were more likely to choose dominated plans.
Subsequent plan switching reduced but did not eliminate dominated choice and widened some disparities.
Hypothetical-choice experiments suggest that poor understanding of cost-sharing and plan value played a central role.
Strong insurance competence was associated with near-elimination of dominated choices in the experimental evidence.

Evidence and methods
The empirical setting is a large U.S. firm with 23,894 employees choosing among plans that shared the same insurer, services, and network but varied in deductible, copayment, coinsurance, out-of-pocket maximum, and premium.
The paper then uses hypothetical-choice experiments to distinguish explanations. Simplifying the menu did not eliminate dominated choice. Making dominance clear reduced dominated choices sharply. Measures of insurance understanding strongly predicted whether participants avoided dominated plans.
Why it matters for Digital Nudging
This paper gives the strongest welfare-warning in the choice-aid cluster. People can actively choose and still choose options that no plausible risk preference can justify. In such contexts, observed choice is poor evidence of Chooser Welfare.
For AI as Choice Aid, the lesson is not simply “recommend the cheapest plan.” The better lesson is that choice aids must build competence: explain deductibles, premiums, worst-case exposure, dominated options, and tradeoffs in a way users can actually use.
The paper also matters for equity. If misunderstanding is socially patterned, then digital choice architecture that assumes competence can widen welfare losses for lower-income users.
Links into the wiki

Behavior-Welfare Gap: active choice can diverge sharply from welfare.
comparison friction (Smart Disclosure): plan comparison requires more than available information.
Smart Disclosure: health-plan data need to be standardized and translated into usable comparisons.
Chooser Welfare: the paper challenges simple revealed-preference interpretations of welfare.

Open questions
Should digital insurance choice aids merely explain dominated options, warn strongly, or prevent enrollment in dominated plans?
Bibliographic reference
Bhargava, S., Loewenstein, G., & Sydnor, J. (2017). Choose to lose: Health plan choices from a menu with dominated options. The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 132(3), 1319-1372. doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjx011

sources/binns,-2018.title: Binns, 2018
sources/binns,-2018.content:
Binns, 2018: Fairness in Machine Learning: Lessons from Political Philosophy
Summary
Reuben Binns argues that fair machine learning cannot define fairness or bias by technical statistical criteria alone. Statistical definitions such as demographic parity, equality of opportunity, accuracy equity, disparate mistreatment, and counterfactual fairness each presuppose normative ideas about discrimination, equality, justice, responsibility, and legitimate grounds for differential treatment.
The paper is the course’s first explicit bridge from fairness metrics (Algorithmic Fairness) to political philosophy. It does not reject formalization. Instead, it argues that formalization has to be guided by the philosophical question: what kind of equality, discrimination, or injustice is at stake in this specific decision context?
Key claims

Fair machine learning faces a prior conceptual problem: before technical mitigation begins, one must decide which fairness ideal is appropriate for the context.
Metric conflict is not only a mathematical inconvenience. It reveals deeper normative disagreement about what fairness requires.
“Discrimination” and “fairness” are not interchangeable. Some algorithmic harms may be morally serious without fitting classic philosophical accounts of wrongful discrimination.
Mental-state accounts of discrimination do not transfer easily to algorithmic systems because algorithms do not possess animus, contempt, or disrespect in the way human decision-makers do.
Accounts centered on “treating people as individuals” also face difficulty because predictive systems necessarily generalize, and generalization is not always wrongful.
Binns treats fairness in fair ML as a placeholder for multiple egalitarian concerns rather than a single technical property.
Relevant egalitarian questions include the currency of equality, spheres of justice, luck and desert, deontic or historical justice, and representational harms.

Evidence and methods
The paper surveys political-philosophical theories and maps them onto fair ML debates. It connects existing technical measures to older debates about discrimination, egalitarianism, equality of opportunity, luck egalitarianism, Rawlsian and Dworkinian resources, Senian capabilities, Andersonian democratic equality, Walzerian spheres of justice, and recognition or representation.
The argument is conceptual rather than empirical. Binns shows that different technical metrics implicitly answer different philosophical questions: whether fairness is about equal outcomes, equal opportunities, accuracy, individualized treatment, counterfactual worlds without protected-class membership, protection from brute luck, political equality, or cultural representation.
Why it matters for Digital Nudging
Digital nudging systems increasingly classify, rank, recommend, score, and personalize. Binns is crucial because these systems often import a fairness metric as if it were a neutral technical choice. In digital environments, that is especially dangerous: the same model may allocate attention, opportunity, visibility, friction, surveillance, or persuasion, and each of those goods may belong to a different sphere of justice.
For the course, this paper shifts algorithmic fairness from “which metric should we optimize?” to “which philosophical account of fairness explains the relevant harm?” That matters for recommendation systems, content moderation, ranking, personalization, targeted nudges, and platform governance, where distributional harms and representational harms often overlap.
Links into the wiki

algorithmic fairness as political philosophy (Algorithmic Fairness): the main concept extracted from the paper.
fairness metrics (Algorithmic Fairness): Binns explains why metrics need normative justification.
Fairness Impossibility Results: metric incompatibility creates a need for philosophical choice.
COMPAS controversy (Algorithmic Fairness): Binns helps interpret why COMPAS cannot be resolved by statistical analysis alone.
Algorithmic Fairness: connects metric choice to accountable institutional design.

Open questions

Which political-philosophical theories should be foregrounded for each digital nudging domain: ranking, recommendation, risk scoring, content moderation, and targeting?
How should Binns be sequenced with Hellman on the moral significance of different errors?
How should the course distinguish distributive fairness from representational fairness in platform settings?

Bibliographic reference
Binns, R. (2018). Fairness in machine learning: Lessons from political philosophy. In S. A. Friedler & C. Wilson (Eds.), Proceedings of the 1st Conference on Fairness, Accountability and Transparency (PMLR Vol. 81, pp. 149-159). PMLR. proceedings.mlr.press/v81/binns18a.html

sources/chang-et-al.,-2024.title: Chang et al., 2024
sources/chang-et-al.,-2024.content:
Chang et al., 2024: Does Counting Change What Counts? Quantification Fixation Biases Decision-Making
Summary
Does Counting Change What Counts? studies how numeric representation changes decisions involving tradeoffs. Across 21 experiments, people tend to favor the option that dominates on the dimension presented numerically, even when the competing qualitative dimension is equally relevant.
The authors call this pattern quantification fixation (Behavior-Welfare Gap). Its mechanism is comparison fluency: numbers are easier to compare than qualitative descriptions, pictures, or visualizations, so decision-makers overweight the quantified attribute.
Key claims

Quantification changes what counts in decision-making.
When one dimension of a tradeoff is numeric and another is qualitative, people privilege the numeric dimension.
The effect appears across managerial, policy, consumer, hiring, and charitable donation contexts.
Quantification fixation persists even when qualitative information is familiar or explicitly mapped to numeric values.
The effect has real consequences in incentive-compatible hiring and donation tasks.
Comparison fluency is a key mechanism: numeric information feels easier to compare.
People with higher subjective numeracy are more susceptible because they feel more comfortable using numbers.

Evidence and methods
The paper reports 21 preregistered experiments with more than 23,000 participants. Main-text studies include hotel, restaurant, hiring, donation, and policy scenarios. The authors randomize which tradeoff dimension is represented numerically and which is represented qualitatively.
The effect is not explained by recall, precision, familiarity, or ambiguity alone. Making numeric information less fluent attenuates the effect, and subjective numeracy moderates it.
Why it matters for Digital Nudging
Digital choice environments constantly translate the world into numbers: ratings, stars, scores, ranks, percentages, counts, dashboards, risk estimates, prices, and algorithmic confidence. This paper warns that quantification is not neutral information architecture. It changes salience and weight.
For AI as Choice Aid, the lesson is subtle. A choice aid should simplify and compare, but it should not make only the numeric dimensions fluent. If an AI system makes price, risk, efficiency, popularity, or predicted satisfaction vivid while leaving dignity, fit, quality, care, or meaning qualitative and vague, it may systematically skew choice.
Links into the wiki

quantification fixation (Behavior-Welfare Gap): the core concept introduced by the paper.
Choice Architecture: numeric representation is itself a design choice.
Smart Disclosure: standardized data help comparison but may overweight quantified attributes.
Behavior-Welfare Gap: easier-to-compare choice can diverge from better choice.

Open questions
How should AI choice aids make qualitative values comparison-fluent without flattening them into misleading scores?
Bibliographic reference
Chang, L. W., Kirgios, E. L., Mullainathan, S., & Milkman, K. L. (2024). Does counting change what counts? Quantification fixation biases decision-making. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 121(46), e2400215121. doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2400215121

sources/coglianese-and-crum,-2024.title: Coglianese and Crum, 2024
sources/coglianese-and-crum,-2024.content:
Coglianese and Crum, 2024: Taking Training Seriously
Summary
Taking Training Seriously connects emerging AI regulation to the technical stage at which models are trained and developed. Coglianese and Crum argue that major governance frameworks, including the EU AI Act, U.S. executive initiatives, and ISO risk-management standards, share a management-based AI regulation (Algorithmic Governance) logic: instead of trying to specify every permitted or forbidden AI output in advance, they require organizations to build internal systems for identifying, managing, documenting, and mitigating risks.
The paper’s distinctive move is to say that this regulatory model should push oversight upstream. Human oversight should not be treated only as post-deployment monitoring, user review, or after-the-fact audit. For high-stakes AI, the training process itself should be designed to include human guidance.
Key claims

AI is heterogeneous and dynamic enough that rigid, prescriptive regulation will often miss the relevant risks.
Management-based regulation is becoming the practical governance paradigm because it requires developers and deployers to maintain internal risk-management systems.
Human oversight is most effective when it shapes training and development, not only deployment.
Human-guided training can improve model performance by adding human intuition, domain judgment, salience, and evaluation criteria that data-only training may miss.
Human-guided training can also support fairness and explainability because it can align models with human-recognizable reasons, examples, and errors.
High-stakes contexts should lean more heavily on human-guided training than low-stakes contexts because the costs of misalignment, opacity, and unfairness are larger.

Course use
Use this paper as the bridge between governance and model construction. It helps the course avoid a narrow view of “oversight” as a dashboard, audit, or appeal button added after a system is already built. For digital nudging, the equivalent point is that ethical governance should enter the design, training, ranking, personalization, and testing pipeline itself.
This paper also gives a constructive complement to the darker Hypernudge concerns. If digital choice architecture becomes adaptive and algorithmic, the response is not only disclosure or prohibition. One response is to require human judgment and domain-specific values to be built into the development process.
Why it matters for Digital Nudging
Digital nudging systems are increasingly trained systems: recommender models, ranking models, personalization engines, generative assistants, and decision-support tools. If their behavioral effects are shaped during training, then governance that begins only after deployment arrives too late.
The paper supplies a strong principle for the course: digital nudges should be governed across the lifecycle, including data selection, training feedback, objective choice, evaluation, deployment, monitoring, and revision.
Bibliographic reference
Coglianese, C., & Crum, C. R. (2024). Taking training seriously: Human guidance and management-based regulation of artificial intelligence. arXiv:2402.08466. arxiv.org/abs/2402.08466

sources/coglianese-and-crum,-2025a.title: Coglianese and Crum, 2025a
sources/coglianese-and-crum,-2025a.content:
Coglianese and Crum, 2025a: Leashes, Not Guardrails
Summary
Leashes, Not Guardrails rejects the common metaphor of AI “guardrails.” Guardrails imply fixed barriers that keep a technology within a bounded lane. Coglianese and Crum argue that this is a poor fit for AI because AI is too heterogeneous, dynamic, and innovative to be governed mainly by static constraints.
The alternative metaphor is the leash. A leash allows movement and exploration, but only if a human retains control of the handle. In regulatory terms, this means management-based AI regulation (Algorithmic Governance): a flexible system that requires developers and deployers to identify risks, design controls, document decisions, audit performance, and maintain human oversight throughout the lifecycle.
Key claims

Guardrails are unrealistic when the technology is highly dynamic and its use paths cannot be specified in advance.
Guardrails can also be unwise if they block beneficial innovation or force all systems into fixed paths.
AI should not be left unregulated; serious harms can arise from irresponsible or ill-managed development and use.
Regulatory leashes combine flexibility with active human oversight.
Management-based regulation is the institutional form of the leash: it governs organizations by requiring internal risk-management systems.
Human oversight can appear through auditing, information disclosure, human-guided training, and human-AI teaming.
A leash regime can fail if oversight becomes pro forma, so regulators must define documentation, auditing, and accountability requirements.

Course use
Use this source as a quick metaphorical and institutional anchor. It is especially useful when students are tempted to think of AI regulation as a menu of banned features, safe design standards, or content filters. The paper says: for dynamic AI systems, governance must track the organization, its processes, and its ongoing grip on the system.
Why it matters for Digital Nudging
Digital nudging often happens through systems that change: feeds, ranking models, adaptive defaults, generative assistants, and A/B-tested interfaces. A guardrail approach may catch some dark patterns, but it will not govern continuous personalization and optimization well.
The leash metaphor gives the course a way to ask whether a platform has a humanly accountable grip on its behavioral systems: what risks it tracks, what objectives it permits, what evidence it collects, how it audits experiments, and when humans can intervene.
Bibliographic reference
Coglianese, C., & Crum, C. R. (2025). Leashes, not guardrails: A management-based approach to artificial intelligence risk regulation. Risk Analysis. doi.org/10.1111/risa.70020

sources/coglianese-and-crum,-2025b.title: Coglianese and Crum, 2025b
sources/coglianese-and-crum,-2025b.content:
Coglianese and Crum, 2025b: Regulating Multifunctionality
Summary
Regulating Multifunctionality argues that foundation models and generative AI intensify the basic problem of AI heterogeneity. A foundation model is not a single-purpose tool with one predictable risk profile. It is closer to a Swiss Army knife: the same underlying system can be adapted to many tasks, domains, users, and harms.
That multifunctionality makes prescriptive, one-size-fits-all regulation especially weak. A rule designed for one use can underreach, overreach, or become obsolete when the same model is used differently. The authors argue that even more flexible tools such as performance standards and ex post liability can struggle because regulators may not be able to monitor all uses or trace harms easily. Their preferred response is management-based AI regulation (Algorithmic Governance): require developers and users to build internal risk-management practices that can adapt to the tool’s changing uses.
Key claims

AI heterogeneity varies across use, design, and problem contexts.
Foundation models increase heterogeneity because one model can support many downstream functions.
Multifunctionality makes fixed design standards and broad prohibitions difficult to calibrate.
Performance standards can fail when performance is hard to define across many uses.
Disclosure and liability can help, but they often face monitoring, information, and enforcement limits.
Management-based regulation is better suited to multifunctional AI because it shifts attention to proactive risk identification, assessment, documentation, mitigation, and revision.
Regulators will need vigilance, agility, technical capacity, leadership, resources, and a culture of regulatory excellence.

Course use
Use this paper to name why digital nudging is not governed well by simple lists of allowed and forbidden interface features. The same recommender, assistant, or personalization engine can inform, persuade, exploit, exclude, explain, or distract depending on its context and objective.
The paper also helps explain why foundation models complicate the course’s later material. LLMs can become choice architects, advisors, tutors, sales agents, compliance tools, emotional companions, and decision aids. The behavioral and ethical risk is not inherent in one function but emerges from the use-case ecology.
Why it matters for Digital Nudging
Digital nudging increasingly depends on multifunctional AI systems. A chatbot can be a disclosure interface in one context, a persuasive sales assistant in another, and a bureaucratic gatekeeper in a third. That makes the ethical evaluation of digital nudging more context-sensitive and more organizational.
For the course, this paper supports a governance thesis: when digital choice architecture is multifunctional, the central regulatory object is not only the interface or the model, but the risk-management system that decides how the model is used.
Bibliographic reference
Coglianese, C., & Crum, C. R. (2025). Regulating multifunctionality. In P. Hacker, A. Engel, S. Hammer, & B. Mittelstadt (Eds.), The Oxford Handbook of the Foundations and Regulation of Generative AI. Oxford University Press. doi.org/10.1093/oxfordhb/9780198940272.013.0011

sources/coglianese-and-lehr,-2017.title: Coglianese and Lehr, 2017
sources/coglianese-and-lehr,-2017.content:
Coglianese and Lehr, 2017: Regulating by Robot
Summary
Regulating by Robot is the legal-defense foundation for algorithmic administration. Coglianese and Lehr ask whether machine-learning tools used for adjudication or rulemaking can fit within constitutional and administrative-law doctrines such as nondelegation, due process, equal protection, reason-giving, and transparency.
Their answer is broadly yes. Properly understood, machine-learning systems need not be unaccountable computerized overlords. They can be treated as extensions of ordinary administrative tools: statistical models, decision aids, instruments, and delegated decision procedures that remain governed by humanly specified objectives, validation, and legal constraints.
Key claims

Administrative agencies can use machine learning in adjudication and rulemaking without necessarily violating constitutional or administrative law.
Nondelegation concerns can be addressed when algorithms are tied to an intelligible principle: an objective function, statutory goal, or policy criterion specified by humans.
Due process analysis should be pragmatic, especially under balancing frameworks such as Mathews v. Eldridge.
Transparency and reason-giving do not require full intuitive access to every internal computation if agencies can explain the system’s objective, data, validation, and role in the decision.
Equal protection concerns depend on how models are designed, trained, validated, and used, not simply on the fact that they are algorithmic.
Algorithmic tools may reduce some forms of arbitrary human discretion, but they create new risks around opacity, validation, and institutional responsibility.

Legal doctrines unpacked

Nondelegation: the concern is that public authority might be shifted from legally accountable officials to an algorithmic system, vendor, or technical process. Coglianese and Lehr respond that machine-learning systems can satisfy the relevant concern when humans specify the intelligible principle: the statutory goal, policy criterion, prediction target, or objective function that guides the system.
Mathews v. Eldridge: the due-process framework asks how much procedure is required by balancing the affected private interest, the risk of erroneous deprivation and value of additional safeguards, and the government’s administrative interest. For algorithmic decision-making, this makes due process a question of stakes, error, safeguards, and institutional role rather than a categorical ban on machine learning.
Equal protection: the question is not whether the decision-maker is algorithmic, but whether the system’s data, features, labels, validation, thresholds, deployment, or human reliance create legally relevant unequal treatment or unjustified group burdens. This makes the paper a bridge to fairness metrics (Algorithmic Fairness) and sociotechnical fairness (Algorithmic Fairness) without reducing equal protection to any one statistical criterion.
Transparency and reason-giving: agencies need not provide full intuitive access to every internal computation. They must be able to explain the system’s objective, evidence base, validation, limits, and decision role well enough to support accountability and contestation.

Course use
Use this paper before the more recent management-based-regulation papers. It establishes the first step in the argument: algorithmic government is not legally impossible. Once that defense is on the table, the course can move to the design question: what kinds of governance systems make algorithmic administration legitimate?
Why it matters for Digital Nudging
Digital nudging often operates in the borderland between recommendation and decision. This paper helps explain why the institutional setting matters. A predictive score, ranking, or automated suggestion may be lawful and useful, but only if its objective, validation, contestability, and human role can be justified.
For the course, the paper helps connect algorithmic nudging to administrative governance: the problem is not simply whether a system uses AI, but whether the institutional use of AI is legally and publicly accountable.
Bibliographic reference
