Aggressive dark patterns produced stronger effects but also more backlash.
Less educated subjects were more susceptible to mild dark patterns.
Price and stakes did not significantly change acceptance in the studied setup; decision architecture drove behavior more than price.
In the second experiment, hidden information, obstruction, and trick questions were especially effective.

Legal argument
The paper treats dark patterns as a consumer-protection problem, not only a design problem. It argues that many dark patterns may be unfair, deceptive, or otherwise legally problematic. It also proposes that regulators can use firms’ own A/B tests and internal experiments as evidence of manipulation or consumer harm.
This is important for the vault’s continuous optimization and experimentation (Hypernudge) page: optimization data can be a source of accountability as well as a source of manipulation.
Why it matters for Digital Nudging
This paper is the best evidence for the course’s point that decision architecture can dominate ordinary market signals. If a mild interface manipulation doubles acceptance while price changes do not move decisions much, then the “choice” being observed is partly a product of the architecture.
It also clarifies why sludge is a method rather than the definition of a dark pattern. Obstruction and hidden information are effective techniques, but the deeper issue is that the design exploits cognitive limits to produce a result users would not endorse under clearer conditions.
Links into the wiki

Dark Patterns: empirical effect sizes and legal diagnosis.
adversarial choice architecture (Dark Patterns): decision architecture as extraction rather than welfare support.
dark pattern regulation (Dark Patterns): FTC and consumer-protection implications.
Sludge: obstruction and hard-to-cancel patterns.
continuous optimization and experimentation (Hypernudge): A/B tests as both design infrastructure and regulatory evidence.

Bibliographic reference
Luguri, J., & Strahilevitz, L. J. (2021). Shining a light on dark patterns. Journal of Legal Analysis, 13(1), 43-109. doi.org/10.1093/jla/laaa006

sources/mathur-et-al.,-2019.title: Mathur et al., 2019
sources/mathur-et-al.,-2019.content:
Mathur et al., 2019: Dark Patterns at Scale
Summary
Dark Patterns at Scale provides the large-scale empirical anchor for the dark-pattern module. The authors crawled roughly 11,000 shopping websites and documented how deceptive or coercive interface designs appear in ordinary e-commerce.
The paper defines dark patterns as user-interface design choices that benefit an online service by coercing, steering, or deceiving users into unintended and potentially harmful decisions. That definition is crucial for the vault because it combines mechanism and objective: the design steers users, and the steering benefits the service at the user’s expense.
Key findings

The crawl found 1,818 dark-pattern instances on 1,254 websites, or about 11.1 percent of the shopping sites studied.
More popular websites were more likely to contain dark patterns.
The authors identified 15 dark-pattern types grouped into seven categories.
They found 234 instances across 183 websites that appeared deceptive.
They also identified 22 third-party entities offering dark-pattern functionality, showing that manipulation can be productized as a service.

Taxonomy and mechanisms
The seven categories are:

Sneaking: adding, hiding, or delaying information, including sneak into basket, hidden costs, and hidden subscriptions.
Urgency: time pressure through countdown timers or limited-time messages.
Misdirection: directing attention away from the user’s preferred action, including confirmshaming, visual interference, trick questions, and pressured selling.
Social proof: claims about other users’ behavior or testimonials.
Scarcity: low-stock or high-demand messages.
Obstruction: making a task difficult, especially hard-to-cancel flows.
Forced action: requiring enrollment or other actions before the user can proceed.

The paper also codes whether patterns are asymmetric, covert, deceptive, information-hiding, or restrictive. This makes it useful for connecting dark patterns to Sludge, Manipulation, and the later normative analysis in What Makes a Dark Pattern… Dark?.
Why it matters for Digital Nudging
This source turns dark patterns from a set of anecdotes into an empirical platform problem. It shows that exploitative choice architecture is not occasional web clutter. It is detectable at scale, can be supplied by specialized vendors, and is often embedded directly into commercial conversion flows.
For digital nudging, the paper also clarifies why examples matter but should not dominate the course. The examples fix the concept: urgency, scarcity, forced action, hidden costs, and hard cancellation. The general lesson is broader: digital interfaces can use behavioral mechanisms familiar from nudging while optimizing for money, data, or retention rather than chooser welfare.
Links into the wiki

Dark Patterns: empirical evidence and central definition.
dark pattern taxonomy (Dark Patterns): seven categories and 15 dark-pattern types.
adversarial choice architecture (Dark Patterns): service-benefiting steering that harms or frustrates users.
continuous optimization and experimentation (Hypernudge): dark patterns can be productized and tested against conversion metrics.
Privacy and Consent: forced action and privacy-invasive disclosure connect to consent design.

Bibliographic reference
Mathur, A., Acar, G., Friedman, M. J., Lucherini, E., Mayer, J., Chetty, M., & Narayanan, A. (2019). Dark patterns at scale: Findings from a crawl of 11K shopping websites. Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction, 3(CSCW), Article 81. doi.org/10.1145/3359183

sources/mathur-et-al.,-2021.title: Mathur et al., 2021
sources/mathur-et-al.,-2021.content:
Mathur et al., 2021: What Makes a Dark Pattern… Dark?
Summary
What Makes a Dark Pattern… Dark? asks what exactly makes a dark pattern normatively objectionable. The paper argues that the field needs more than lists of examples. It needs a way to connect observable design attributes to the normative reason a design is troubling and to the method used to measure harm.
This makes the paper a systematic complement to the earlier empirical and taxonomy work. It clarifies the difference between description, evaluation, and measurement.
Key claims

Dark patterns modify the decision space and manipulate information flow.
Descriptive attributes include asymmetry, restrictiveness, disparate treatment, covertness, deception, and information hiding.
No single normative lens captures all dark-pattern concerns.
Measurement should match the normative concern being invoked. A study of financial loss, privacy invasion, consumer autonomy, competition, or legal compliance will need different evidence.
Dark patterns should be understood in relation to nudges, sludge, manipulation, and market manipulation rather than as a purely HCI category.

Normative lenses
The paper organizes evaluation around four lenses:

Individual welfare: financial loss, privacy invasion, cognitive burden, wasted time, and frustrated preference satisfaction.
Collective welfare: harms to competition, marketplace trust, and the distribution of burdens across populations.
Regulatory objectives: compliance with consumer-protection, privacy, and data-protection regimes such as the FTC Act, GDPR, CPRA, and related rules.
Individual autonomy: whether the design impairs authorship over one’s own decision by hiding alternatives, exploiting inattention, or making refusal harder to exercise.

Why it matters for Digital Nudging
This source gives the course a way to avoid treating “dark” as a vibe. It asks what value has been impaired and what evidence would show the impairment.
That is especially useful when the course moves from classic nudging to digital nudging. A design can be user-serving under one lens and troubling under another: it may reduce effort while increasing privacy loss, or increase conversion while reducing autonomy. Mathur et al. help separate the mechanical question “what does the interface do?” from the normative question “why is that bad?” and the empirical question “how would we know?”
Links into the wiki

Dark Patterns: core normative framework for the concept.
dark pattern taxonomy (Dark Patterns): attributes and levels of description.
dark pattern regulation (Dark Patterns): legal and regulatory lenses.
Chooser Welfare: individual welfare as one evaluation target.
Manipulation: autonomy and information-flow concerns.
Privacy and Consent: privacy invasion and consent degradation as measurable harms.

Bibliographic reference
Mathur, A., Mayer, J., & Kshirsagar, M. (2021). What makes a dark pattern… dark? Design attributes, normative considerations, and measurement methods. In Proceedings of the 2021 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (pp. 1-18). ACM. doi.org/10.1145/3411764.3445610

sources/mills,-2022.title: Mills, 2022
sources/mills,-2022.content:
Mills, 2022: Personalized Nudging (Mills)
Summary
Personalized Nudging (Mills) gives a systematic framework for understanding what gets personalized in a personalized nudge. Its core contribution is a two-component distinction: choice personalization and delivery personalization.
For this vault, “choice personalization” is also recorded as content or target personalization, because it concerns what the person is nudged toward. “Delivery personalization” concerns how the nudge is delivered or which nudge mechanism is selected.
Key claims

Impersonal nudges can fail because populations are heterogeneous. A nudge that benefits many people may hurt or misfit people with different circumstances.
Personalization is a response to heterogeneity, not merely a synonym for Big Data.
Choice personalization uses heterogeneity data to personalize the outcome or target of the nudge when the nudge mechanism is already selected.
Delivery personalization uses heterogeneity data to personalize the method of nudging, such as selecting a default, social-norm message, reminder, or other nudge type.
The two forms can be combined, as when a system personalizes both the medium of an intervention and the product, action, or option promoted through that medium.
Personalized nudging does not necessarily require Big Data. Some forms can be built with relatively simple data such as birth dates or other temporal landmarks.
More detailed data can expand personalization opportunities, but this increases privacy, access, governance, and accountability burdens.
Personalized nudging can undermine universality, shared social experiences, transparency, and public scrutiny, especially when people receive different regulatory or behavioral interventions.

Two-component framework

Choice or content personalization: personalization within nudges. The architect has selected the nudge type and uses data to determine the best target or outcome. Mills’s example is a savings nudge that uses a personally meaningful “fresh start” date or chooses a different default contribution level for different people.
Delivery personalization: personalization across nudges. The architect uses data to determine which nudge mechanism is most effective for a person. One person may respond to a default; another may respond better to a social-norm message, reminder, or information format.

This distinction is the paper’s durable value for the course. It lets us separate personalization of mechanism from personalization of target.
Relationship to Behavioral Economics 2.0
Mills is conceptually related to Algorithms as a Vehicle to Reflective Equilibrium: Behavioral Economics 2.0, but less radical. Mills systematizes personalization within the nudge paradigm: the architect can personalize what is nudged toward or how the nudge is delivered.
Ludwig et al. push further. Their Behavioral Economics 2.0 (Algorithmic Thought Partners) asks whether algorithms can help determine what direction is right for the person under reflective equilibrium (Algorithmic Thought Partners). Mills therefore complements the programmatic paper by supplying a cleaner vocabulary for the levels at which personalization can occur.
Why it matters for Digital Nudging
This paper helps prevent a common ambiguity in Digital Nudging. When a platform says that a nudge is personalized, it may mean at least two different things:

The system personalized the delivery mechanism, such as timing, channel, frame, salience, or nudge type.
The system personalized the target, such as which option, default, product, contribution rate, or behavior the user is nudged toward.

Those are ethically and technically different. Delivery personalization can improve effectiveness without changing the behavioral target. Content or target personalization can change the welfare claim itself, because the system is asserting that a different outcome is better for this particular person.
The paper also sits between Hypernudge and precision nudging (Personalized Choice Architecture). Like Yeung, Mills treats data-driven personalization as powerful and governance-sensitive. Unlike Yeung, the paper is not primarily a critique of structural harms. It offers a practical conceptual framework for distinguishing kinds of personalization, while still warning about universality, data access, and privacy.
Links into the wiki

personalized nudging (Personalized Choice Architecture): main concept extracted from the article.
Personalized Choice Architecture: broader digital choice-environment concept updated with the two-component distinction.
precision nudging (Personalized Choice Architecture): related concept; often emphasizes delivery precision, but Mills shows that target personalization is distinct.
Behavioral Economics 2.0 (Algorithmic Thought Partners) and reflective equilibrium (Algorithmic Thought Partners): more radical extension that asks what the right target is for the person.
Privacy and Consent and Transparency and Disclosure: policy challenges around data access, data protection, universality, and public scrutiny.

Bibliographic reference
Mills, S. (2022). Personalized nudging. Behavioural Public Policy, 6(1), 150-159. doi.org/10.1017/bpp.2020.7

sources/mullainathan,-2025.title: Mullainathan, 2025
sources/mullainathan,-2025.content:
Mullainathan, 2025: Economics in the Age of Algorithms
Summary
Economics in the Age of Algorithms is a high-level summary and agenda-setting paper for the efficiency branch. Sendhil Mullainathan argues that algorithms are not merely another technology affecting the economy. They change how decisions are studied, modeled, and improved, so they should change economics itself.
For the course, the most important parts are the pretrial decision example, the general category of Prediction Policy Problems, the argument that algorithmic interventions can be unusually cost-effective, and the open problem of designing human-plus-algorithm decision aids.
Key claims for the efficiency branch

Many important social decisions are prediction policy problems: the decision does not primarily ask “what is the causal effect of this intervention?” but “which case has the highest predicted risk, benefit, need, or fit?”
The pretrial bail example remains the anchor. Algorithmic prediction can improve the crime/incarceration frontier: roughly 40 percent lower jailing at the same risk level, or 25 percent lower risk at the same jailing rate.
These results are not an argument for automation. They show that algorithms can discover information that could improve decisions.
The hardest work is econometric rather than computational. Building a supervised learner may be easier than evaluating whether it improves on the human decision-maker.
selective labels (Algorithmic Policy Efficiency) and omitted payoff bias (Algorithmic Policy Efficiency) are the two central evaluation hazards. Ignoring them builds in a pro-algorithm bias.
Algorithms expand the toolkit of behavioral intervention. Decision aids are presented as a category that extends the tradition of nudges and choice architecture.
Human and algorithmic prediction have different comparative advantages: algorithms extract signal from the data frame, while humans may notice information missing from the data frame and may understand the broader payoff function.
Algorithmic interventions can look unusually cost-effective because software scales cheaply, human decision-making leaves room for improvement, and ranking problems create large deadweight loss when cases are misordered.
The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Algorithms is the companion effectiveness paper that quantifies this point with MVPF comparisons across several domains.
Economists must treat algorithm design as part of policy design. Once algorithms mediate job search, health choice, school choice, consumer choice, or social programs, behavioral parameters are no longer external facts; they can depend on the algorithm.

Selective coverage
This note does not try to ingest the whole paper at equal depth. It preserves the parts most useful for the second branch of the course:

prediction policy problems as the general class behind bail, hiring, medical testing, tax audits, credit, job search, and recommender-assisted decisions;
the welfare-frontier interpretation of algorithmic decision support;
the evaluation framework around selective labels and omitted payoffs;
the human-plus-machine framework behind the override problem (Algorithmic Policy Efficiency);
the bridge from algorithmic prediction to digital nudging, behavioral interventions, and LLM-mediated decision support.

Why it matters for Digital Nudging
Digital nudging increasingly uses algorithmic decision aids, recommenders, and AI assistants rather than static interface tweaks. Mullainathan gives the course a way to place those systems in a wider economic frame: they are interventions that change how people and institutions predict, rank, choose, and learn.
The paper also links the efficiency branch to the constructive side of Behavioral Economics 2.0 (Algorithmic Thought Partners). If algorithms can reveal decision mistakes and redesign choice environments at scale, then digital nudging is no longer only about salience, defaults, or friction. It becomes a question of how to build prediction-guided decision systems that improve welfare without collapsing into opaque automation.
Bibliographic reference
Mullainathan, S. (2025). Economics in the age of algorithms. AEA Papers and Proceedings, 115, 1-23. doi.org/10.1257/pandp.20251118

sources/narayanan-et-al.,-2020.title: Narayanan et al., 2020
sources/narayanan-et-al.,-2020.content:
Narayanan et al., 2020: Dark Patterns
Summary
Dark Patterns: Past, Present, and Future is the best compact overview for placing dark patterns in the history of digital nudging. The article argues that contemporary dark patterns emerged from the convergence of three strands: retail deception and manipulation, behavioral economics and nudging, and Silicon Valley growth hacking.
The paper is especially important for the user’s framing because it treats dark patterns as a subversion of nudging. Behavioral insights that were originally defended as helping people make better choices can be repurposed by firms to maximize revenue, data extraction, and engagement.
Key claims

Dark patterns are not merely old tricks placed on screens. Digital systems make them easier to test, scale, personalize, and automate.
Behavioral economics supplies an understanding of cognitive biases, heuristics, defaults, social proof, scarcity, and framing. In dark patterns, those tools are used adversarially.
Growth hacking supplies the optimization culture: interfaces are continuously tested against growth, conversion, retention, and revenue metrics.
A/B testing converts broad behavioral principles into precise operational designs by discovering which wording, timing, colors, and flows work best.
Dark patterns extract money, data, and attention.
Dark patterns can be offered as third-party services, making manipulation modular and reusable.

The historical convergence
The article’s most useful contribution is the three-part genealogy:

Retail deception provides the older market-manipulation repertoire: hidden fees, misleading claims, bait-and-switch tactics, and pressure selling.
Behavioral nudging supplies the scientific and design vocabulary for shaping choices without removing options.
Growth hacking supplies the platform-management objective and experimental infrastructure.

That convergence explains why digital dark patterns are structurally different from isolated deception. They are optimized choice architectures embedded in live systems.
Why it matters for Digital Nudging
This source gives the course a clean formulation of the dark-pattern pivot: digital nudging can become adversarial when the same behavioral machinery is aimed at extraction rather than user welfare.
It also connects dark patterns to continuous optimization and experimentation (Hypernudge). The ethical issue is not only that a single screen is manipulative. It is that firms can run experiments until manipulation becomes subtle enough, profitable enough, or personalized enough to escape ordinary user resistance.
Links into the wiki

adversarial choice architecture (Dark Patterns): the article’s historical synthesis is the backbone for the concept.
Dark Patterns: compact overview of mechanisms and stakes.
continuous optimization and experimentation (Hypernudge): A/B testing and growth hacking as optimization infrastructure.
Sludge: the article connects dark patterns with sludge-like friction, while preserving the broader extraction frame.
dark pattern regulation (Dark Patterns): discusses regulatory responses including consumer protection and data-protection law.

Bibliographic reference
Narayanan, A., Mathur, A., Chetty, M., & Kshirsagar, M. (2020). Dark patterns: Past, present, and future. Communications of the ACM, 63(9), 42-47. doi.org/10.1145/3397884

sources/narayanan,-2026.title: Narayanan, 2026
sources/narayanan,-2026.content:
Narayanan, 2026: What If Algorithmic Fairness Is a Category Error?
Summary
What If Algorithmic Fairness Is a Category Error? is the course’s system-level corrective to the fairness-metrics sequence. Arvind Narayanan argues that the central question is not whether a predictive algorithm satisfies a mathematical fairness property in isolation. The better question is how to design accountable algorithmic bureaucracies: sociotechnical decision systems made of models, data, institutional goals, human discretion, interfaces, thresholds, appeals, incentives, and political context.
The paper does not make fairness metrics useless. It demotes them. Calibration, predictive parity (Fairness Impossibility Results), error rate parity (Fairness Impossibility Results), and related metrics can be diagnostics that alert us to possible discrimination or harm, but they should not be treated as constraints whose satisfaction makes a system fair.
Key claims

Algorithmic decision-making systems do not exist in a vacuum. Their harms and benefits depend on the organizations, legal regimes, user interfaces, and political choices through which predictions become action.
The algorithmic fairness movement has often been drawn to mathematically precise criteria because they make fairness tractable, legally legible, and apparently less political. That tractability is also a limitation.
Fairness is too narrow as a proxy for justice. A system can satisfy a chosen group-fairness metric and still be unjust, invalid, demeaning, unaccountable, punitive, or built around the wrong social goal.
The COMPAS controversy (Algorithmic Fairness) should not only be taught as a metric conflict. Even in a counterfactual world without racial error disparity, pretrial risk detention may still be objectionable as precrime, procedurally opaque, and damaging to already burdened communities.
Fairness metrics should be used as diagnostics for possible sociotechnical discrimination, not as final engineering objectives.
Bias audits can become a bandage for a deeper bandage. In hiring, social services, and criminal justice, checking group disparities in a model may distract from whether the tool is valid, whether the institution should use it, and whether the underlying policy is itself just.
Algorithmic bureaucracies require explicit attention to values and goals, but public administration often works through situated judgment and successive limited comparisons rather than clean objective specification.
Cost-benefit analysis can help compare otherwise hidden trade-offs, but it must account for distribution, nonmarket goods, liberty, dignity, and values smuggled into the analysis.
Human discretion is not just noise to be replaced. Street-level decision makers often supply judgment, contextual knowledge, moral interpretation, and escalation for cases that rules and models do not anticipate.
A future “third wave” of algorithmic accountability should sit between model-level fairness tweaks and very broad structural critique: technical enough to inspect systems, political enough to address institutions.

Conceptual contribution
This paper clarifies the relation among the fairness readings already in the vault:

Inherent Trade-Offs in the Fair Determination of Risk Scores shows why plausible metrics conflict.
On Statistical Criteria of Algorithmic Fairness defends predictive parity as preserving the meaning of scores.
Measuring Algorithmic Fairness shifts attention from belief to action and error burdens.
Fairness in Machine Learning: Lessons from Political Philosophy argues that metric choice depends on normative theory.
Algorithmic Decision Making and the Cost of Fairness argues that fairness criteria must be assessed against regulatory goals and decision costs.
Narayanan then pushes one step further: even normatively justified, policy-aligned metrics are only partial diagnostics unless the whole sociotechnical decision system is evaluated.

Why it matters for Digital Nudging
Digital nudging systems are not merely algorithms. They are choice architectures embedded in platforms, institutions, incentives, data pipelines, feedback loops, A/B tests, recommender systems, human review practices, and governance arrangements. This paper gives the course a vocabulary for saying why fairness in digital nudging cannot be reduced to a ranking metric, a recommender accuracy score, or an equalized error rate.
For Hypernudge, the paper reinforces the concern that algorithmic steering operates through opaque systems rather than isolated decisions. For constructive Behavioral Economics 2.0 (Algorithmic Thought Partners), it adds a design challenge: algorithmic thought partners and personalized choice architectures should be assessed as sociotechnical systems, including what they optimize, what they explain, when they escalate, how users contest them, and whether they genuinely support agency.
Bibliographic reference
Narayanan, A. (2026). What if algorithmic fairness is a category error? In S. Nyholm, A. Kasirzadeh, & J. Zerilli (Eds.), Contemporary debates in the ethics of artificial intelligence (pp. 77-96). Wiley-Blackwell.

sources/schmidt-and-engelen,-2020.title: Schmidt and Engelen, 2020
sources/schmidt-and-engelen,-2020.content:
Schmidt and Engelen, 2020: The Ethics of Nudging: An Overview
Role in the vault
The Ethics of Nudging: An Overview is an excellent review map for the ethical debate around nudging. Its main value is not a new ethical test, but an organized account of what the major objections are, how defenders of nudging respond, and why no single objection defeats the nudge program as a whole.
The review is especially useful for the course because it turns the broad worry that nudges undermine autonomy into a set of more precise questions. A nudge can preserve external freedom of choice while still raising concerns about whether the chooser’s action reflects their own ends, whether the intervention respects rational agency, and whether the choice architect exercises uncontrolled power.
Core argument
The case for nudging rests on several familiar claims: nudges can be cost-effective, evidence-driven, comparatively freedom-preserving, politically attractive, and responsive to the inevitability of Choice Architecture. But the inevitability argument is not a blank check. Deliberate choice architecture is ethically different from accidental influence because intentional design brings responsibility for goals, mechanisms, evidence, avoidability, side effects, and institutional control.
The review’s conclusion is deliberately balanced. There is no knockdown objection showing that nudging as a whole should be rejected. At the same time, the objections are not distractions. They identify the criteria that should guide case-by-case assessment of particular nudges.
Ethical objection map
The review divides autonomy objections into four dimensions:

Freedom of choice: do options remain externally available, and is avoidance practically possible?
Volitional autonomy: does the nudge help people act on their own ends, or does it make their choices less genuinely theirs?
Rational agency: does the nudge bypass or exploit deliberation, or can it improve the match between people, decision procedures, and environments?
Non-domination: is the architect’s power transparent, democratically controlled, and contestable, or does it become uncontrolled influence over citizens or users?

This map clarifies why “options remain open” is not enough. A nudge can preserve formal choice while still raising concerns about ownership of ends, rational respect, opacity, or domination.
The review then treats Manipulation and dignity as worries that are best decomposed through the earlier autonomy questions. If manipulation is troubling because it works behind people’s backs, exploits vulnerability, bypasses rational capacities, or infantilizes adults, the response must address transparency, rational agency, autonomy, and non-domination rather than simply insisting that choice remains formally free.
Ends and structural reform
Some objections concern the goals nudges pursue rather than the psychological route by which they work. The epistemic worry is whether policymakers know what is good for people. The moral worry is whether governments should promote contested ends in pluralist societies. The review’s response is comparative: these questions apply to many policy tools, not only nudges, and nudges may sometimes be preferable because they preserve opt-out. But easy opt-out can also make paternalistic expansion seem too easy, so transparency and democratic control remain important.
The structural-reform objection is equally important. Nudging can be misused as a light-touch substitute for stronger action on socioeconomic, institutional, or market causes of harm. The best response is not to deny the problem, but to treat nudging as one policy instrument among others. Nudges can be combined with structural reform, used in nonideal contexts where stronger reform is unavailable, or directed at structural mismatches between human decision-making and intentionally designed environments.
Digital choice architecture
The review explicitly identifies digital choice architecture as a fertile and underdeveloped area for future ethics work. Digital nudges are especially powerful because firms can collect user data, run A/B tests, use algorithms, personalize interventions, and shape behavior at scale. They are also especially difficult to scrutinize because technical details, optimization objectives, and machine-learning decisions may be opaque to users and outsiders.
This makes the source a bridge from classical nudge ethics to Hypernudge, Dark Patterns, Privacy and Consent, and platform governance. The public-private contrast becomes central: public nudges may be transparent and democratically controlled, while private digital choice architecture may be proprietary, personalized, and optimized for attention, conversion, or data extraction.
Why it matters for Digital Nudging
The review gives the course a compact ethical diagnostic for digital nudges:

Do not ask only whether options remain available; ask whether choice remains meaningful across autonomy, rational agency, and domination.
Do not treat transparency as a generic notice; ask whether users and publics can understand, contest, and control the relevant influence.
Do not treat manipulation as a vague insult; ask what kind of bypassing, opacity, vulnerability exploitation, or dignity failure is alleged.
Do not let the light-touch appeal of nudging displace stronger remedies when the problem is structural, exploitative, or market-made.
Do not evaluate digital choice architecture only at the visible interface; include data collection, experimentation, personalization, algorithmic opacity, and institutional incentives.

This source therefore strengthens Ethics of Nudging as a review framework and helps prepare the move from classical nudging to digital nudging.
Links into the wiki

Ethics of Nudging: supplies the main objection map for the concept page.
Nudging and the Ethics of Nudging: reinforces the synthesis claim that ethics is plural and case-specific.
Nudge: clarifies that intentional choice architecture raises responsibility even when choice architecture is unavoidable.
Manipulation: reframes manipulation and dignity as concerns about opacity, rational agency, autonomy, and domination.
Transparency and Disclosure: adds non-domination and democratic control to the transparency discussion.
Hypernudge: provides a classical-ethics bridge to data-driven, personalized, opaque digital choice architecture.

Bibliographic reference
Schmidt, A. T., & Engelen, B. (2020). The ethics of nudging: An overview. Philosophy Compass, 15(4), e12658. doi.org/10.1111/phc3.12658

sources/sunstein,-2016.title: Sunstein, 2016
sources/sunstein,-2016.content:
Sunstein, 2016: The Ethics of Influence: Government in the Age of Behavioral Science
Role in the vault
The Ethics of Influence: Government in the Age of Behavioral Science is the main ethics framework for the course’s opening treatment of nudging. It complements Nudge: The Final Edition by asking when behaviorally informed influence is legitimate, when it is required, and when it becomes objectionable.
The book is especially useful for Digital Nudging because digital interfaces intensify the ethical problems Sunstein analyzes: influence can be hidden in interface structure, optimized by experimentation, personalized with user data, and shielded from public scrutiny by proprietary systems.
Structural map

Chapter 1, “The Age of Behavioral Science”: maps the rise of behavioral public policy and argues that choice architecture is unavoidable.
Chapter 2, “Choice and Its Architecture”: extends the choice-architecture argument and introduces transparency, visibility, and the difference between System 1 and System 2 influence.
The Ethics of Influence - Chapter 3 As Judged by Themselves: priority chapter on chooser-centered welfare.
The Ethics of Influence - Chapter 4 Values: priority chapter on welfare, autonomy, dignity, and self-government.
The Ethics of Influence - Chapter 5 Fifty Shades of Manipulation: priority chapter on manipulation, consent, transparency, and democratic authorization.
The Ethics of Influence - Chapter 6 Do People Like Nudges: important empirical chapter on public support, reactance, trust, and value alignment.
The Ethics of Influence - Chapter 7 Green by Default: important applied chapter on default rules, active choosing, and personalization.
Chapter 8, “Mandates”: mapped as a comparison point between nudges and requirements.

Central claims
Sunstein’s starting point is that Choice Architecture cannot be avoided. A government, platform, institution, or firm must decide what to show, what to default, what to simplify, what to make salient, and what happens if people do nothing. The ethical question is therefore not whether influence exists, but how influence is justified and constrained.
The central normative standard is that many nudges should make people better off as judged by themselves. This becomes Chooser Welfare in the vault: interventions should not merely increase compliance, engagement, revenue, or behavior change, but should plausibly help people pursue ends they would endorse under conditions of adequate information and reflection.
Sunstein organizes the ethics of nudging around four values: welfare, autonomy, dignity, and self-government. Welfare asks whether the intervention improves people’s lives. Autonomy asks whether people retain meaningful agency, not just formal option sets. Dignity asks whether people are treated respectfully rather than as objects of control or humiliation. Self-government asks whether public influence is transparent, accountable, and open to scrutiny.
The book also develops a strong caution against Manipulation. Manipulative influence is not just influence that works; it is influence that insufficiently engages people’s capacities for reflective and deliberative choice. Transparency helps, but transparency does not automatically make manipulation acceptable.
Why it matters for Digital Nudging
Digital nudging often happens in environments where users cannot easily see the choice architecture, infer the architect’s goals, or compare alternative designs. Defaults, rankings, recommendations, disclosures, notifications, cancellation flows, consent banners, and onboarding sequences can all steer behavior while looking like ordinary interface plumbing.
Sunstein’s framework gives the course a way to separate legitimate digital nudges from darker forms of steering:

Does the design serve the user’s welfare as judged by the user, or does it optimize a proxy such as engagement, conversion, data capture, or retention?
Is the nudge easy to notice, understand, and resist, or is it buried inside a proprietary algorithm or interface flow?
Does the system preserve autonomy in a practical sense, including attention, time, comprehension, and exit?
Does the design respect dignity, or does it shame, trick, exhaust, or infantilize users?
Is there enough transparency, accountability, and contestability for affected users, regulators, or the public to evaluate the influence?

The proprietary character of many digital systems makes the self-government value harder to satisfy than in classic public nudging. The course implication is that private and platform-based nudges need ethics tests that include not only intention and outcome, but also inspectability, data access, optimization objectives, and institutional accountability.
Concepts seeded or updated

Ethics of Nudging
Chooser Welfare
Manipulation
Transparency and Disclosure
Nudge
Choice Architecture
Defaults
Sludge

Bibliographic reference
Sunstein, C. R. (2016). The ethics of influence: Government in the age of behavioral science. Cambridge University Press.

sources/sunstein,-2022.title: Sunstein, 2022
sources/sunstein,-2022.content:
Sunstein, 2022: Governing by Algorithm? No Noise and (Potentially) Less Bias
Summary
Governing by Algorithm? No Noise and (Potentially) Less Bias gives the algorithmic-governance cluster a behavioral-law argument for why administrative agencies should take algorithms seriously. Sunstein distinguishes two sources of human error: bias and noise. Bias is systematic error in a particular direction; noise is unwanted variability across or within decision-makers. Human administrators, judges, prosecutors, doctors, and other officials can exhibit both.
The article’s constructive claim is that well-designed algorithms can eliminate noise and reduce some cognitive biases because they apply the same rule to identical cases and rely on statistical predictors rather than intuitive shortcuts. The caution is that algorithms can still be biased, especially when inputs, targets, or outcomes reflect discrimination. Sunstein therefore does not defend algorithmic governance as automatically legitimate. He argues that algorithms can improve administrative decision-making when they are properly designed, evaluated, and constrained by legal and policy goals.
Key claims

Human administrative judgment is vulnerable to cognitive biases such as availability bias, anchoring, affect-driven judgment, optimism bias, present bias, and current-offense bias.
Human systems are also noisy: similarly situated people may receive different outcomes because of occasion noise, level noise, or pattern noise.
Algorithms are “silent” in Sunstein’s sense: the same algorithm does not treat identical cases differently because of the day, decision-maker, sequence of prior cases, mood, or local salience.
Eliminating noise is morally and administratively important because random variation creates unequal treatment and increases total error.
Algorithms can counteract cognitive bias in prediction problems by giving appropriate statistical weight to information that humans over- or underweight.
The bail example from Human Decisions and Machine Predictions shows the point: algorithmic ranking could reduce crime at the same detention rate or reduce detention at the same crime rate.
Discrimination remains a distinct problem. Algorithms can encode or perpetuate discrimination through biased inputs, proxy variables, historically contaminated labels, or prediction targets that are themselves infected by discrimination.
A major virtue of algorithms is that they can make tradeoffs more explicit: agencies and publics can see what happens when a system is constrained for accuracy, detention, racial balance, or other policy goals.

Evidence and examples
Sunstein uses the administrative state as the main institutional setting. Asylum adjudication illustrates noise: outcomes may vary sharply depending on the adjudicator, sequence of prior decisions, or other irrelevant factors. Pretrial bail illustrates the efficiency case: judges overweight the current charge and release many defendants whom the model identifies as high risk, while detaining some lower-risk defendants.
The article distinguishes two kinds of bias. Cognitive bias is a prediction error produced by heuristics or intuitive judgment. Discriminatory bias is unequal treatment or impact connected to legally and morally salient groups. Algorithms are especially promising for the first, but require careful legal and policy scrutiny for the second.
Course use
Use this article as a compact supplement to Regulating by Robot and Administrative Law in the Automated State. Coglianese and Lehr explain why algorithmic administration can fit administrative-law doctrine; Sunstein explains why agencies might want algorithmic tools in the first place: to reduce noise, correct cognitive bias, and make prediction-policy tradeoffs more explicit.
It also belongs beside Algorithmic Policy Efficiency. Sunstein does not replace the econometric argument in Human Decisions and Machine Predictions or Fragile Algorithms and Fallible Decision-Makers. He gives that argument a legal-behavioral frame: the relevant comparison is not algorithm versus ideal human judgment, but algorithmic decision support versus actual human systems that are noisy, biased, and institutionally consequential.
Why it matters for Digital Nudging
Digital nudging often uses algorithms to rank, recommend, target, warn, personalize, or triage. Sunstein’s article helps separate two questions that the course should keep apart. First, can an algorithmic system reduce human error by improving prediction and consistency? Sometimes yes. Second, can that same system reproduce discrimination, omit relevant values, or make the wrong policy tradeoff? Also yes.
For the course, this is useful because it resists both algorithmic enthusiasm and algorithmic rejection. Digital choice architecture can be better than human-only choice architecture when it reduces noise and cognitive bias. But its legitimacy depends on objectives, inputs, validation, discrimination analysis, policy alignment, and the broader sociotechnical decision system.
Links into the wiki

Algorithmic Governance, Management, and the Automated State: synthesis page where this article reinforces the positive case for algorithmic administration.
Algorithmic Policy Efficiency: connects Sunstein’s noise-and-bias argument to the efficiency frontier in prediction policy.
Algorithmic Fairness: keeps the discrimination warning tied to model inputs, targets, impacts, and institutional use.
fairness as policy alignment (Algorithmic Fairness): captures Sunstein’s point that algorithms can reveal tradeoffs among policy goals rather than settle them automatically.

Open questions
How should the course distinguish useful consistency from harmful rigidity when an algorithm eliminates administrative noise but also reduces opportunities for mercy, individualized treatment, or empathic escalation?
Bibliographic reference
Sunstein, C. R. (2022). Governing by algorithm? No noise and (potentially) less bias. Duke Law Journal, 71(6), 1175-1206.

sources/sunstein,-2023.title: Sunstein, 2023
sources/sunstein,-2023.content:
Sunstein, 2023: Behavioral Biases, Choice Engines, and Paternalistic AI
Summary
Behavioral Biases, Choice Engines, and Paternalistic AI asks how AI-powered “choice engines” might help consumers make better decisions when ordinary choice is distorted by limited information, present bias, inertia, limited attention, or other behavioral biases.
The paper starts from the problem of Chooser Welfare under heterogeneity. Average behavioral interventions can help some people and hurt others. Home energy reports, graphic labels, calorie labels, defaults, taxes, mandates, and bans may have different effects across groups. The fact that an intervention improves average behavior does not show that it improves each chooser’s welfare.
Choice engines are Sunstein’s constructive response. A user-facing AI tool could recommend products, plans, or defaults that fit a person’s own situation, values, and constraints. It could offer simple rankings such as Good, Better, and Best; explain relevant tradeoffs; make future costs salient; and help users incorporate internalities and, where appropriate, externalities.
Key claims

Behavioral interventions are welfare-relevant only when they address real mistakes, not merely when they change behavior.
Heterogeneity makes mass nudges, labels, taxes, mandates, and bans risky: the same intervention can help one group while burdening another.
Present bias, limited attention, status quo bias, unrealistic optimism, and inadequate information can create internalities: costs people impose on their own future selves.
AI choice engines might reduce internalities by helping people compare total costs, future consequences, and personal fit.
Choice engines can range from nonpaternalistic menus to mildly, moderately, or highly paternalistic systems.
The ethically attractive version preserves freedom of choice while making welfare-relevant information and recommendations easier to use.
Choice engines can also be dangerous: they may be self-interested, manipulative, biased, coarse, or insufficiently informed about the user’s actual preferences.
Rules against dominated options, shrouded attributes, deception, and manipulation may be needed around AI choice aids.

Evidence and examples
Sunstein uses several examples to show both promise and danger:

Retirement-plan engines that automatically enroll employees or screen out unsuitable plans.
Motor vehicle and appliance choice engines that make future fuel or energy savings salient.
Good/Better/Best recommendation formats for users who want simplicity.
“Keep It Simple” versus “Tell Me Everything” versions of an aid, depending on how much information a user wants.
Possible “light patterns”: friction such as “are you sure?” prompts or multiple clicks when the system predicts that a choice is harmful.
Dominated retirement or consumer options, high-fee plans, and shrouded attributes as cases where choice engines need oversight.

Why it matters for Digital Nudging
This is a bridge source for AI as Choice Aid. It takes the classical nudge problem, “people often choose badly in complex environments,” and asks what happens when the choice architect becomes an AI assistant rather than a static form, label, or default.
For the course, the important move is not that AI should replace choice. It is that AI can make the welfare standard more operational. Instead of inferring welfare from what people click, buy, or fail to change, a choice engine can help users compare consequences, surface hidden costs, and decide under better conditions.
The paper also preserves the ethical tension. A choice engine can be an algorithmic thought partner, but it can also become a personalized dark pattern if the builder optimizes for fees, conversion, data capture, or engagement.
Links into the wiki

AI as Choice Aid: synthesis thread on AI and digital tools that support welfare-sensitive choice.
Behavior-Welfare Gap: the gap between observed behavior and chooser welfare.
Algorithmic Thought Partners: a broader constructive category for user-serving AI decision support.
Smart Disclosure: data infrastructure that choice engines can use.
Shrouded Attributes: hidden product terms and add-ons that choice engines can surface.
adaptive armor (Algorithmic Thought Partners): the defensive version of AI choice support in adversarial markets.

Open questions
How paternalistic can an AI choice engine become before it ceases to be a choice aid and becomes a system for delegated control?
Bibliographic reference
Sunstein, C. R. (2023). Behavioral biases, choice engines, and paternalistic AI (Preliminary draft, August 12). SSRN. ssrn.com/abstract=4539053

sources/thaler-and-sunstein,-2021.title: Thaler and Sunstein, 2021
sources/thaler-and-sunstein,-2021.content:
Thaler and Sunstein, 2021: Nudge: The Final Edition
Work overview
Nudge: The Final Edition is the core popular statement of Richard H. Thaler and Cass R. Sunstein’s case for nudging, choice architecture, and libertarian paternalism. For the Digital Nudging course, its most reusable contribution is not the catalog of policy examples, but the framework: choices are always presented in some designed environment; Humans predictably depart from the Econ model; and private or public choice architects can use that knowledge either to help choosers or to exploit them.
The book defines nudges as choice-architectural interventions that predictably alter behavior while preserving options and avoiding large changes in economic incentives. It argues that the benchmark for welfare is what choosers would choose under fuller attention, information, cognitive ability, and self-control, not what the architect happens to prefer.
Structure of the work







































































UnitCourse priorityIngest statusCourse usePreface to the Final EditionimportantmappedExplains what changed in 2021: Smart Disclosure, Sludge, personalized defaults, curation, and updated digital examples.Nudge - Introductionfoundationalsubstantially ingestedDefines choice architecture, libertarian paternalism, and nudges.Nudge - Part I Humans and Econsfoundationalsubstantially ingestedProvides the behavioral economics foundation: heuristics, self-control, and social influence.Nudge - Chapter 4 When Do We Need a Nudgefoundationalsubstantially ingestedGives the diagnostic test for when nudges are useful.Nudge - Chapter 5 Choice Architecturefoundationalsubstantially ingestedGives the main design toolkit for choice architects.Chapter 6, But Wait, There’s MoreimportantmappedExtends the toolkit with additional design principles.Nudge - Chapter 7 Smart Disclosureimportantsubstantially ingestedDirectly relevant to digital consumer choice, data portability, and choice engines.Nudge - Chapter 8 Sludgeimportantsubstantially ingestedDirectly relevant to dark patterns, administrative burden, cancellation flows, and privacy consent.Parts III-IV, Money and Societyperipheral for first course passmappedUseful source of assignment examples, especially savings defaults, organ donation, climate, insurance, and credit.Chapter 15, Much Ado About NudgingimportantmappedFrames autonomy, manipulation, transparency, active choice, boosts, and the limits of nudges.
Central theses

Choice Architecture is unavoidable: websites, forms, menus, defaults, disclosures, rankings, and physical layouts all organize attention and action.
Humans are not Econs. People use heuristics, exhibit biases, face self-control problems, and respond to social influence, especially when decisions are hard, rare, delayed, opaque, or poorly supported by feedback.
A Nudge should preserve freedom of choice: it should be easy and cheap to avoid, should not ban options, and should not rely on major material incentives.
The best nudges are often mundane: defaults, reminders, simpler forms, better mappings, timely feedback, salient warnings, and carefully structured choice sets.
Markets do not automatically correct behavioral vulnerability. Firms may profit from inattention, optimism, inertia, or confusion, especially in digital settings where friction can be asymmetric.
The same design knowledge can support welfare or exploitation. Sludge, dark patterns, hidden opt-out costs, shrouded prices, and manipulative consent flows are the book’s internal warning signs.
Nudges are not a complete policy philosophy. Thaler and Sunstein accept that taxes, subsidies, mandates, and bans are sometimes necessary, especially when choices harm others or when nudges are too weak.

Major concepts introduced

Nudge
Choice Architecture
Behavioral Economics
Defaults
Smart Disclosure
Sludge

The book also supplies reusable source-local ideas that may later deserve concept pages: libertarian paternalism, active choosing, prompted choice, mappings, channel factors, error-forgiving design, planner/doer conflict, mental accounting, social norms, choice engines, personalized defaults, curation, and the publicity principle.
Important units
Nudge - Introduction should anchor the opening definition of the course. It gives the cafeteria example, the claim that there is no neutral design, the definition of choice architect, and the criteria that distinguish nudges from bans, mandates, taxes, and subsidies.
Nudge - Part I Humans and Econs should be used as the compact behavioral economics background. The point is not to teach every bias, but to show why digital environments can steer behavior: attention is limited, defaults stick, framing matters, self-control varies by state, and social signals travel quickly.
Nudge - Chapter 4 When Do We Need a Nudge supplies the course’s diagnostic checklist: scarce attention, difficulty, delay, infrequency, poor feedback, and unclear mapping from choice to welfare.
Nudge - Chapter 5 Choice Architecture supplies the design toolkit most transferable to digital interfaces: make it easy, use defaults carefully, expect error, give feedback, improve mappings, structure complex choices, and make incentives salient.
Nudge - Chapter 7 Smart Disclosure and Nudge - Chapter 8 Sludge are the most digital-ready chapters in the final edition. They connect classic nudging to machine-readable data, user data portability, choice engines, cookie banners, cancellation flows, and administrative burdens.
Internal tensions or debates
The book insists that choice architecture is unavoidable, but that claim does not settle what choice architects are entitled to do. Digital environments intensify the tension because the same interface affordances can produce helpful guidance, aggressive persuasion, dark patterns, or opaque manipulation.
Thaler and Sunstein favor welfare as judged by choosers themselves, but digital platforms often infer welfare from behavior, engagement, retention, or willingness to pay. That creates a gap between revealed behavior and well-being that the course should keep visible.
The authors defend transparency and the publicity principle, while also acknowledging that some nudges work through salience, ease, and default effects that users may not explicitly notice. For digital nudging, this tension is central to autonomy, consent, and interface governance.
The book treats active choice as a useful alternative to defaults in some settings, but also warns that forcing choice can itself become burdensome choice architecture. This is crucial for privacy consent, cookie banners, app onboarding, and account settings.
Why it matters for Digital Nudging
This source gives the course its starting vocabulary. Digital nudging can be understood as choice architecture implemented through interfaces, data, defaults, prompts, rankings, disclosure systems, reminders, recommendations, consent flows, and friction. The book also gives the course an ethical baseline: a nudge should preserve real exit, be easy to resist, and improve choices by the chooser’s own lights. When digital systems make opting out hard, hide costs, or steer users toward platform-serving outcomes, the same framework identifies them as Sludge or darker choice architecture rather than welfare-oriented nudges.
Bibliographic reference
Thaler, R. H., & Sunstein, C. R. (2021). Nudge: The final edition. Penguin Books.

sources/yeung,-2017.title: Yeung, 2017
sources/yeung,-2017.content:
Yeung, 2017: Hypernudge: Big Data as a Mode of Regulation by Design
Summary
Hypernudge: Big Data as a Mode of Regulation by Design is the vault’s cornerstone source for the shift from classic nudging to Digital Nudging. Yeung argues that Big Data decision-guidance systems are a form of design-based regulation: they configure the informational environment in which people choose, while leaving the final decision formally with the user.
The paper’s central concept is Hypernudge. Unlike static nudges, hypernudges are networked, continuously updated, dynamic, pervasive, and personalized. They operate through recursive feedback loops that monitor behavior, update profiles, and reconfigure the user’s informational Choice Architecture in real time.
Key claims

Big Data is both a technology and a process: it mines large data flows for patterns, converts them into predictive analytics, and applies those analytics to new cases.
The paper distinguishes automated decision-making from digital decision-guidance. Hypernudging belongs to decision-guidance: the system offers suggestions, rankings, or prompts, while the person remains the formal chooser.
Big Data decision-guidance works as informational choice architecture. Search rankings, recommendations, navigation suggestions, and feeds shape what users see, notice, compare, and treat as relevant.
Hypernudging is powerful because it combines personalization with continuous modification. The system can update the target’s choice environment based on individual behavior, broader environmental data, and population-wide trends.
The feedback loop also generates more data for the choice architect, which can be stored, repurposed, and fed into other Big Data applications.
Hypernudges are soft but not weak. They can be unobtrusive, pervasive, difficult to resist, and deployed at massive scale.
Notice and consent are inadequate safeguards because privacy policies are unread, hard to understand, constantly outpaced by new data uses, and poorly suited to cumulative privacy harms.
Hypernudging raises concerns about manipulation, deception, democratic participation, privacy, autonomy, algorithmic opacity, commercial self-interest, and surveillance capitalism.

Crucial digital features

Personalization: the user’s choice environment is tailored through data profiles, predictions, and inferred preferences.
Continuous modification: the system can update both standards and behavioral interventions as new data arrive.
Recursive feedback: user behavior becomes input for further optimization.
Pervasiveness: digital services can shape routine choices across search, social media, navigation, commerce, entertainment, and administration.
Scale: one algorithmic adjustment can affect millions of users simultaneously.
Opacity: the operative mechanism may be hidden in machine-learning models, ranking systems, trade secrets, or platform experiments.

Course themes opened by the article

Recommendation Systems as informational choice architecture.
continuous optimization and experimentation (Hypernudge), including A/B testing and live algorithm changes.
Dark Patterns and manipulative design, especially when influence is hidden or commercially self-serving.
Algorithmic Fairness, including black-box systems, bias, predictive policing, and search engine power.
Privacy and Consent, especially the failure of notice-and-consent models under Big Data conditions.
Transparency and Disclosure, because public or contractual disclosure does not make dynamic algorithmic influence intelligible.
Chooser Welfare, because optimization targets such as engagement, relevance, convenience, or revenue may not track the user’s reflective interests.

Why it matters for Digital Nudging
This source marks the course’s pivot from digital examples of classic nudges to digital nudging as a structurally different mode of power. In the earlier vocabulary, a nudge changes the choice architecture while preserving options. Yeung shows that digital systems can do this continuously, personally, algorithmically, and invisibly.
For the course, the key move is that digital nudging is not just “nudging on screens.” It is data-driven regulation by design. A recommender, search engine, feed, navigation system, or app interface can monitor users, infer likely responses, adjust what is made salient, and learn from the result. That makes the ethical questions from The Ethics of Influence: Government in the Age of Behavioral Science and Nudge and the Manipulation of Choice much harder: transparency, consent, manipulation, and user welfare must be evaluated in systems that are dynamic, proprietary, and personalized.
Links into the wiki

Hypernudge: main concept extracted from the article.
Personalized Choice Architecture: captures personalization as a core feature of digital nudging.
continuous optimization and experimentation (Hypernudge): captures recursive feedback, A/B testing, and real-time modification.
Recommendation Systems: captures search, ranking, feeds, and recommender engines as choice architecture.
Privacy and Consent: captures the failure of notice and consent as a safeguard.
Algorithmic Fairness: captures black-box accountability and bias concerns.
Dark Patterns: captures the manipulative design direction opened by hypernudging.

Bibliographic reference
Yeung, K. (2017). “Hypernudge”: Big Data as a mode of regulation by design. Information, Communication & Society, 20(1), 118-136. doi.org/10.1080/1369118X.2016.1186713

syntheses/ai-as-choice-aid.title: AI as Choice Aid
syntheses/ai-as-choice-aid.content:
AI as Choice Aid
The constructive case for AI in digital nudging begins from a negative finding: what people choose often fails to reveal what would make them better off. Choices can be distorted by inattention, misunderstanding, self-control problems, poor feedback, comparison costs, hidden fees, misleading salience, and internal conflict between impulsive and reflective selves. In digital environments, the problem becomes sharper because platforms can observe behavior in detail and optimize around it. But observable behavior is not the same as welfare.
This synthesis treats AI as a possible choice aid: a tool that helps people understand, compare, reflect, and act in ways closer to their own considered interests. The point is not that AI is automatically welfare-enhancing. The same capacities can become hypernudging, dark patterns, or engagement traps. The central question is when AI repairs the Behavior-Welfare Gap rather than exploits it.
The behavior-welfare problem
The classical revealed-preference assumption says that what people choose is evidence of what they want. This is often useful, but the sources in this cluster show why it can break.
Choose to Lose is the cleanest example. Employees at a large firm chose among health plans that were otherwise identical except for financial cost-sharing and premiums. Many low-deductible plans were financially dominated by high-deductible alternatives: no plausible health-spending scenario or standard risk preference could justify them. Yet 61% of employees chose nominally dominated plans, with substantial avoidable spending. The likely explanation was not a subtle preference for insurance, but low insurance competence.
Comparison Friction shows a milder but equally important version. Medicare Part D beneficiaries could access personalized plan-cost comparisons, but many did not. A mailed letter that delivered personalized cost information increased switching and reduced predicted costs. Information existed, but it was not psychologically or practically available enough.
The Challenge of Understanding What Users Want gives the platform version. Users may spend a long time with content and later regret it. Engagement can reflect value, but it can also reflect moreishness, habit, or a System 1 pull that no longer serves reflective welfare. Even a platform trying to maximize user utility can fail if it observes only engagement.
Together these cases make the same point: behavior is evidence, not welfare itself.
Why information is not enough
Many policy and interface responses rely on disclosure. The user is told the fee, shown the plan, given the privacy terms, or pointed to the comparison website. Disclosure: Psychology Changes Everything explains why this often disappoints. Limited attention, motivated attention, complexity, delay, overload, probability misperception, and social pressure can prevent disclosure from improving decisions. Disclosures can even backfire when they morally license conflicted advisors or burden recipients with information they cannot use.
The useful lesson is not anti-disclosure. It is anti-formalism. Good disclosure must be simplified, standardized, comparative, timely, vivid where appropriate, and often mediated by intermediaries. This is exactly where digital and AI tools become relevant. They can turn disclosure into sense-making: reading the terms, comparing the options, calculating the user’s likely costs, explaining why one option dominates another, and helping the user act.
But comparison itself can distort. Does Counting Change What Counts? shows that people overweight numeric dimensions because numbers are comparison-fluent. A choice aid that makes only prices, ratings, probabilities, or efficiency scores fluent may cause users to neglect qualitative dimensions such as fit, dignity, care, trust, or meaning. The design target is not “more numbers.” It is balanced intelligibility.
Markets can be adversarial
Shrouded Attributes explains why choice aids are needed in markets where firms profit from consumer mistakes. A firm can advertise a low base price while shrouding expensive add-ons, fees, or penalties. Sophisticated consumers may exploit the low base price and avoid the add-ons, while myopic consumers pay. Competition does not necessarily unshroud the market because educating consumers may benefit competitors as much as, or more than, the educating firm.
This matters for digital nudging because many online interfaces are built around the same structure: visible benefits, delayed costs, hidden renewals, late fees, hard-to-compare bundles, opaque privacy costs, or cancellation burdens. In such settings, an AI choice aid is not merely a convenience tool. It can become adaptive armor (Algorithmic Thought Partners): a user-side system that surfaces hidden attributes, summarizes terms, compares total costs, and resists strategic obfuscation.
The danger is that the aid itself may be funded, ranked, or optimized by actors with conflicting incentives. A comparison tool can become a paid placement system. An AI assistant can become a sales agent. The ethics of choice aids therefore depends on institutional incentives as well as interface quality.
From prediction to choice aid
Digital choice aids often begin as prediction systems. They infer what a person might click, buy, watch, choose, or prefer from past behavior and from the behavior of similar users. That predictive capacity is useful, but it does not settle the welfare question.
The first problem is target selection. If the target is engagement, purchase, retention, or acceptance, the system may be accurate while still missing welfare. The second problem is interpretation. A predicted preference can encode confusion, impulse, inertia, or manipulation as easily as considered endorsement.
For the course, this distinguishes ordinary Recommendation Systems from Algorithmic Thought Partners. A recommender predicts what the user or similar users will like, click, buy, or watch. A choice aid helps the user reason about what they should do by their own lights. Sometimes prediction helps; sometimes it reproduces the very behavior that needs correction.
Choice engines and paternalism
Behavioral Biases, Choice Engines, and Paternalistic AI names the constructive instrument: the choice engine. A choice engine can ask what matters to a user, compute the consequences of options, incorporate future costs, and present a simple set of recommendations such as Good, Better, and Best. It can be more personalized than a mass nudge and less coercive than a mandate.
The hard question is paternalism. A choice engine may simply organize information, or it may recommend, default, warn, add friction, or block options. Some of these moves can be justified when options are dominated, shrouded, or predictably harmful. But the same moves become dangerous when the system is coarse, biased, self-interested, opaque, or overconfident about welfare.
The design standard should therefore be stronger than behavioral effectiveness. A choice aid should improve decisions under conditions the user could endorse: better information, clearer comparisons, reduced manipulation, preserved exit, and explanation adequate for trust.
Design principles
The sources converge on a small set of design principles for AI choice aids.
First, do not equate behavior with welfare. Engagement, retention, purchase, plan inertia, and acceptance are starting points for inquiry, not final welfare measures.
Second, make comparison usable. Personalized, standardized, action-guiding comparisons matter more than passive information access.
Third, build competence. In complex domains such as insurance, the aid should explain the structure of the choice, not only output a recommendation.
Fourth, surface hidden attributes. Fees, add-ons, renewal terms, privacy costs, penalties, and long-run consequences should move from the periphery to the decision surface.
Fifth, explain enough for contestability. Users need to understand the relevant reasons, assumptions, and tradeoffs, especially when the aid asks them to defer to algorithmic judgment.
Sixth, keep qualitative values in view. Simplification should not turn the easiest-to-number attribute into the only attribute that counts.
Seventh, audit incentives. A choice aid built by a platform, seller, insurer, or affiliate network may optimize for conversion, revenue, or retention while presenting itself as user-serving assistance.
Course payoff
AI as choice aid is the constructive counterpart to the dark-pattern and hypernudge warnings. Digital systems can personalize, test, rank, recommend, and adapt continuously. Those capacities can exploit attention, extract data, and maximize engagement. They can also help people make sense of complex options, resist shrouding, avoid dominated choices, and act on their own considered interests.
The hinge is welfare. If AI systems merely learn what people do, they may scale mistakes. If they help people understand what they would endorse under better conditions, they can become a genuine extension of nudging’s original paternalistic aspiration: not just changing behavior, but helping choosers by their own lights.
